div.p: Here, then, is what I have to set before you concerning the figures and the virtues out of which political oratory is composed, by which it is judged, and through which it is advanced as something of great worth — composed, as it were, out of parts, member by member, so that from every side it stands complete and self-sufficient in itself. These figures are of the following kinds and the following number: dignity, gravity, amplitude, credibility, vehemence, emphasis, force, elaborateness, sweetness, clarity together with purity, brevity together with conciseness, and chastening of style.

Dignity, then, is in general constituted in three ways: by the thought, by the figure, and by the diction. By "thought" I mean the sense and the conceptions in which the subject matter is found; by "figures" I mean the mould of the discourse, in which the thoughts, as they are brought out, make the discourse appear of this or that character. And these figures have the greatest power in discourse — as much power as living, moving things have over things that are otherwise. By "diction" I mean the very wording by which the conceptions are delivered.

Gravity arises, in general, as to thought and as to figure, but as to diction scarcely at all. As to thought, then, gravity arises thus: when one is led to accuse oneself, or one of one's own household or friends; for such a thing would be grave, since one might rather have praised; or, in general, one of those persons on whose behalf, or to whom, one is speaking — as Demosthenes: "I have meddled too far, and so has the city that was persuaded by me; let all the errors and wrongs be mine."

Amplitude arises, in general, as to thought, as to figure, and as to diction. As to thought, thus: when one takes up indefinite matters along with the definite, for instance: "From many sources, then, one might discern his folly and his malice" — this is the indefinite taken on from without; now the definite: "but not least from what he said about fortune." And again: "Many disadvantages, then, I for my part suffer in this contest from Aeschines" — this is indefinite; now the definite taken up in a sum: "but two of them, men of Athens, and great ones"; then he divided these by species: "one, that I do not now contend for an equal stake; the other, that which all men have by nature — to hear gladly abuse and accusations, but to be vexed at those who praise themselves." For all these things belong to amplitude: the taking on of the indefinite — "Many disadvantages, then, I for my part suffer"; the gathering into a sum — "but two of them, men of Athens, and great ones"; the dividing by species — "one, that the contest is not for an equal stake; the other, that all men are so disposed as to hear gladly those who abuse, but to be vexed at those who praise themselves." And a third example: "In many cases, men of Athens, one might seem to me to see the goodwill of the gods becoming manifest to the city"; then the leading on to the definite: "but not least in the present circumstances." And again: "Many, then, of the things done by that man are worthy of praise; but the greatest of all is the raising of the walls."

Credibility arises in two ways: as to thought and as to figure. As to thought, thus: when one first establishes one's own just claims as being true and easy to demonstrate, as in the speech Against Aristocrates: "I have supposed, men of Athens, that the speech is a very small and easy matter, concerning the proof that the decree has been moved contrary to this law."

Vehemence arises in three ways: as to thought, as to figure, as to diction. And as to thought, thus: when one rebukes distinguished persons, for instance: "You have departed, men of Athens, from the post in which your ancestors left you." And another like this: "For you alone of the Greeks keep quiet." And again: "And of these things you yourselves are the cause, having allowed them, in the first place, after the Persian wars to strengthen their city." You produce vehemence also when you do not shrink from disparaging distinguished matters or persons, for instance: to praise one's ancestors is a most distinguished thing, but how did Demosthenes at once at the outset disparage it? "Those who praise your ancestors seem to me to speak a gratifying speech, but not one that does service to those very men whom they extol." And in general, to rebuke has vehemence, as in those words: "Both seem to me to err — both those who have spoken for the Arcadians and those who have spoken for the Lacedaemonians."

In a certain way the three virtues of discourse — vehemence, emphasis, and harshness — though they differ in name, yet in power have very much in common with one another in most cases: for vehemence is an emphatic kind of discourse, and harshness can produce vehemence. Nevertheless, as to thought, you will produce emphasis when you state matters continuously and one upon another, as in the speech Against Leptines: "He defeated the Lacedaemonians in a sea-battle, and took forty-nine triremes captive, and captured most of the islands, and brought here three thousand persons captive, and declared a hundred and ten talents from the enemy"; and again: "Seventeen cities he took, seventy triremes he captured, a hundred and ten talents he declared, so many trophies he set up." Each of these is a fact in itself; but the bringing of one continuously upon another has produced the emphasis.

Force arises only in one way, as to thought; and if anyone supposes it to arise in any other respect, he greatly errs. Force is when one arranges beforehand, from afar, something useful to oneself, as in the speech Against Aristocrates Demosthenes, wishing to show that it is perilous and against the city for one of the Thracian kings to become master, takes it up from afar and establishes that the weakness of Cersobleptes, whose general Charidemus is, is itself a safeguard of the Chersonese; so that, conversely, there is danger to the Chersonese if most of the kings are overthrown and the whole power comes round to the one, Cersobleptes, through Charidemus. From afar, then, he arranged beforehand that to decree that the slayer of Charidemus be liable to seizure makes Cersobleptes formidable, and he, once grown great, will overthrow the other kings, through whom the Chersonese is preserved: "And that it may become quite plain to you from the very things said: it is necessary, first of all, to state and show what it is that has made you hold the Chersonese securely; for through learning this you will clearly see the wrong as well. It is this, then, men of Athens: that on the death of Cotys, Berisades and Amadocus and Cersobleptes became three kings of Thrace instead of one; for it has come about that these are rivals to one another, while they court and conciliate you. Certain men, then, wishing to put a stop to this, and to overthrow the other kings and hand over the whole rule to Cersobleptes, contrive that this preliminary decree be passed in their favour."

Elaborateness arises, in general, in three ways: as to thought, as to figure, as to delivery. As to thought, when one does not separate the thoughts from one another nor set them apart, but joins them to one another; and when one uses mixed and manifold conceptions, as it were drawing them in from without and seizing upon them from what remains; and when one does not set forth the matters bare, but with the things that attend upon them and with the nature of the matters — for instance, telling the manner, or the time, or the cause, or the place; and when one uses tropes, elaborateness arises.

Sweetness arises, in general, in three ways: as to thought, as to figure, as to delivery. As to thought, thus: when one uses conceptions drawn from without, for instance from histories and proverbs and fables.

Clarity and purity arise as to thought, as to figure, and as to delivery. As to thought, thus: when one does not invert the order of the matters, but goes through them in the order in which they were done; and when one does not throw in from without any thoughts upon them, but goes through the very things that were done; and when one goes through the known as known and the disputed as disputed.

Brevity and conciseness arise as to thought and as to diction. As to thought, thus: when one at once binds oneself to the necessary points of the matters, and when one does not treat everything as primary, but treats some things as primary and others not so.

The discourse is chastened, in general, in three ways: as to thought, as to figure, as to diction. As to thought, thus: when one does not give way to conceptions drawn from without; and when, compelled to use some conception, one does not introduce it simply, but marks that one was compelled, and tends to it; and when one does not simply set down thoughts severed from the subject matter, but as close to it as possible.

Composition is of three kinds: the continuous, that which is strung out in sequence through several members, as: "For a disease, men of Athens, has fallen upon Greece, a grievous one"; the loose, sometimes diffused, as: "Let it be; let these things come about; I make no objection"; and that by period, which is a structure of clauses and phrases rounded off into a complete sense, as: "And, accounting them both serious, men of Athens, and necessary for the city, I shall try to say about them what I think to be expedient."

"Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles son of Peleus." For it is the work of the Muses to go through with precision the wrath with which Achilles was wrathful at Troy and the things that befell from it; for they were neither slight nor few, but this, the most grievous of the things of the war, came upon the Achaeans: for many of them, good men, were destroyed before their time, and to many it did not fall even to obtain burial, but the dogs made an end of them as they lay. And it was the plan of Zeus, and not by mere chance did so many things fall together, beginning from when first Achilles son of Peleus and Agamemnon son of Atreus, king of the Greeks, fell into strife. Which, then, of the gods set them at odds, and from what shall we say the strife began? From Apollo, who cast a plague upon the Achaeans in anger at their king; and the cause of it was this. A certain old man came, Chryses by name, to the camp of the Achaeans, a priest of Apollo, to ransom his captive daughter, who was in the keeping of Agamemnon, holding a golden staff and on the staff the fillets of the god, bringing too not the least of ransoms; and he supplicated all the Achaeans, but especially the sons of Atreus, praying together with them that they might take Troy and be saved home, but that to himself it might fall to ransom the girl, and that it altogether befitted them to revere the god. Thereupon all the rest received his words and shouted assent to give the child back to the priest; but Agamemnon would not give her up, and threatened besides that if he caught him either lingering now or coming again hereafter for the same purpose, his supplication would not avail him, and the words would no longer be on behalf of the child, but for his own safety; and her he would not release, but would keep her in Argos as a wife, plying his household tasks all her life; but if he wanted any safety, let him go at once. Hearing this, the priest was afraid and immediately departed in silence; but when he was at a distance from the camp, he sent up every cry, calling on Apollo as Sminthian, Tenedian, Chrysean, Fair-bowed, naming all his names: "If ever, master, I either offered you sacrifice or roofed a temple to please you, let this now be granted me in return for those things: to wipe off these tears upon the Achaeans' own bodies; and may you come upon them as an archer." The god receives his prayers and at once set out for the punishment.

Since we have set before you the figures of political oratory and its virtues, you must now hear also about the form of the simple style; for there is nothing one ought to consider so much as the qualities of the simple and plain style and its differences from the political and contentious style. This is no easy matter, since all discourse is of one genus and one nature; nevertheless there are certain variations and forms that differ from one another.

The conceptions, again, in regard to expression, belong to the simple writers — for instance, to use, should it so chance, even rather undistinguished conceptions. At any rate, when Xenophon wished to establish that Cyrus is a man of great worth, consider how he managed it. For the proposition is political, and the proofs most political — that Cyrus came to be of great worth; but of the conceptions some were political, some simple. Political are such as these: "Cyrus came to be of great worth, for he most easily accomplished the hardest thing." And what is the hardest thing? To rule over men. Thus far the establishing is political. If, then, you were handling it politically, you would have said thus: "Cyrus came to be of great worth, for he accomplished what was hardest — to rule over men. Why? Because men are not readily willing to be ruled, but many lordships and many tyrannies have been overthrown by those unwilling to be ruled." Thus far the conceptions are political.

The simple discourse too must be varied, especially in such a kind, and in one place to produce dignity, in another amplitude, in another standing, in another to display character and grace, and in another even laughter, if possible — as it is here too: "Philip the jester, knocking at the door." For the character is very graceful, which is the mark of simple discourse; for to strip away the designs and to use the very words and to follow the nature of the matters, and not to fear their smallness and lowliness, belongs to a plain and noble soul, whence too the arts of discourse were discovered, by which it was able to take on magnitude even for things that do not have magnitude by nature; and sometimes the things made manifest in them are such, while others even make manifest something false, as this too: "You are always mocking us, because you have given Protagoras much money for wisdom." For this makes manifest a slight grace, and at the same time has a certain malice in it.

Character has dignity also in making manifest either piety toward the gods or benefactions toward friends; and one must attend most of all to such things, for the greatest and most numerous of the observations are taken according to these conceptions. And the conceptions are taken from the things in the matter itself; but to have the conceptions stated as about piety and good obedience belongs very much to the purpose of the simple writers. For they do not, as I said, much delight in using the hypothetical, unless necessity somewhere arise — for instance, "one must be pious, one must obey ruling gods" — but, as it were, they sketch certain conceptions of how one must act, not saying didactically that one must not do this, but, in general, "to those who do these things, such things are wont to result."

The sweetness of diction, we have said, is supplied from comedy and Plato and Xenophon; and the simple writers use also poetic diction, when they wish to clothe the discourse of the observations with bulk, and from comedy. It belongs to it to begin from partitions and as from an addition: "and yet," "and indeed," "but then," "but indeed"; for such things furnish simplicity to the discourse.

The simple discourse takes on beauties also from places, should it so chance, and from other attendant things, for instance, when one calls a city great and prosperous, when a river, or whence it flows, how great its breadth — such things always add beauty to the discourse. To go through by species all that attaches to a thing, whether to a river or a city or a plain, breaks up the simplicity; but the generic, if "great and prosperous," preserves both the beauty and the plainness.

The greatest thing in simple discourse is that it should seem as true as possible, and that the things said should appear to be such as anyone might think easy to conceive. This comes about most of all when one takes a conception from the very matter introduced — for instance, as in the Agesilaus, he says, "that he wished to make war spending the King's resources rather than the resources of the Greeks." For taking from what was done by Agesilaus — and his crossing into Asia was about to take place — this conception, through which he showed him to be prudent, he seemed to have spoken most truly about him.

The economy of a discourse is, in everything, the fitting arrangement and the expectation of what is said, and the thoughts and the arguments depending on one another and holding to the subject; and besides these the other observations, all that belong to simple economy. I say, then, that if there is one heading, one must, without anticipation, state the distinguished points in its favour, and so set down the anticipation, having taken up beforehand something distinguished against the adversary; then thus, if they bring anything against ourselves too, consider. If the things from the adversary are more, one must consider the matter; for the method is the same; for the heading is that one must make the things of the enemies, being weak, to appear so, and the things in our own favour far surpassing; for it is plain to all how it would come about, and could be no otherwise.

Concerning interpretation I would say only this: to use neither noun nor verb otherwise than those from the books; and this you might say thus simply — not to put all things in all kinds, but each one separately according to the dignity proper to simplicity, to passion, to character, to spirit. And the parts of the Demosthenic discourses contribute much to the form of interpretation; but everywhere in expression Xenophon alone works simplicity. For spirit or passion or anger or sharpness and all the other things that are stirred belong to dignity or harshness, but to the changing and exhortation of the passions, such as the judgement of Demosthenes is; and the use of examples is Socratic, yet such a thing does not suit the political discourse very well.

Of the arguments, Demosthenes always, and those who have compiled forensic discourses, make selections and distinctions, and mark, heading by heading, setting down their forces — doing this with reason, both because their discourse is contentious, so that the hearers may at once learn their strength and be able to examine each thing accurately.

Come, then, let us learn also about the beginning of the discourse, in what manner Xenophon is wont to make his beginnings. One must, in all discourses alike, arrange beforehand what is useful about the matters, and either resolve the things that oppose, or establish them for oneself. In this, then, it is alike with the political; but the idioms are left to the simple in the handling and the delivery.

Most of all the difference of the matters makes a difference toward each kind of discourse; for instance, the political men do not raise doubts about distinguished and well-known matters or persons, but the historical writer, raising doubts and hesitating even over distinguished things, works simplicity.

As to thought, then, your discourse will be dignified when it is drawn from elevated conceptions; and conceptions are elevated, in a word, when one makes use of distinguished matters, when something is said about distinguished subjects, and when one treats of what is rare and ancient. Distinguished, first of all, are matters concerning the gods, as when you trace your ideas back to things divine — the goodwill of the gods, the kindness of fortune; as, for example, in many cases one seems to me to see the goodwill that comes from the gods, and the like.

But where you are able, beyond all doubt, to prove that you are doing no wrong, there to use such boldness as to deprive yourself of the pardon or kindness that comes from the judges, as when you say: "Do not endure even a word from me, not even if I have administered all public affairs supremely well; but rise up and condemn me at once" — gravity arises here too. And concerning a friend likewise gravity arises, if you deprive him of either the pardon or the kindness of the judges. Gravity arises also when you call down something monstrous upon yourself, as: "Yet I would rather have died than have said these things."

Amplitude is also this: when you set forth the matters generically, and then go through them by species, as in the speech Against Leptines. What he wishes to introduce is this: "It is not, then, only that Leucon should not be wronged that we must consider, but Epicerdes also." But before stating the species — "but Epicerdes also" — he took up the generic beforehand: "but anyone else as well who, having done you good in his prosperity, has now come to a time when it is needful for him to receive immunity from you." Then he came to the species, having marked it off: "Who, then, is this? Epicerdes the Cyrenaean." And again, introducing the benefactions of Epicerdes, he took up the generic beforehand and then introduced the species: "but for the sake of so great a crisis, in which it was hard even to find one of the very men who had been benefited willing to remember by whom he had been served." Now he tells what this man did, by species: "For this man gave a hundred minae to those of the citizens who had met with misfortune in Sicily." And again, generically: "Such and so great buildings and adornment of temples and harbours and the like did they leave us, that to none who came after has any room for surpassing them been left." Then by species: "the Propylaea here, the Parthenon, the dockyards." And again, in the speech Against Leptines, wishing to scrutinize and discredit those who supported the law, he first mentioned them generically: "Advocates have been chosen to defend the law, and these the men most skilled in speaking"; then by species: "Leodamas of Acharnae and Cephisodotus of Cerameis"; then again generically, gathering it together: "But hear what you might justly suppose against these men"; then again by species: "first, against Leodamas." Whenever, then, you do not state the species bare, but take up beforehand the generic, you produce amplitude.

Credible also is to make the things in dispute appear more conspicuous than the things demonstrated and admitted, as in the speech Against Aristocrates, where, having demonstrated the illegality, with the matter of the inexpedience still remaining to be examined, he credibly took it up and made out the inexpedience to be even plainer than the illegality — the thing in dispute plainer than the thing demonstrated — where he says: "For the decree is so very contrary to the laws that it is more inexpedient than illegal."

And to disparage distinguished persons as being in an absurd condition produces vehemence, for instance: "But you, the people, unstrung, with your money and your allies serving in the rank of an attendant and an appendage."

Emphasis is produced also by marking the qualities, where he says: "a dreadful sight"; and again: "a disease dreadful and grievous, needing much watchfulness and correction at your hands." And in the speech Against Meidias: "But what — both dreadful, men of Athens, and monstrous to me at least — seems to have been done by this man as an impiety, not merely a wrong."

Force is also to do away beforehand, before stating a point, with something from afar that opposes it. "How, then, was it that, having perceived from your speaking together with Philocrates that I had taken bribes, you who had been elected to our embassy stayed to serve as envoy with us, and did not swear off?" Against this, having set the objection without a formal statement of it, he then brought in the solution: "For I had agreed with the captives to bring them ransom, and on this account I went on the second embassy, to ransom them and save them so far as I could; it was a dreadful thing, then, to lie and abandon men who were citizens in their misfortune." It would have seemed to be a formal statement, and a fabrication shifted to fit what had happened; but as it is, before setting down the statement, he took up beforehand the matter of the captives by the comparison of the dates: "In the time we spent in Macedonia, what did each of us choose to do? I, for my part, to rescue the captives and search them out and spend money of my own; but this man — you will presently hear what he persisted in doing." Having in this way arranged beforehand the matter of the captives, he now brings forward the statement itself upon the solution already prearranged: "And when this man presently says to you, 'Why, then, Demosthenes, as you allege, having known from my speaking with Philocrates that we were doing nothing sound, did you serve again on the later embassy, the one about the oaths, and not swear off?' — remember this, that I had agreed with those whom I myself ransomed that I would come and bring ransom and save them so far as I could; it was a dreadful thing, then, to lie and abandon men who were citizens in their misfortune."
As to figure, elaborateness arises thus: by the use of partitions.
As to figure, sweetness arises when one uses novel modes of delivery.
As to figure, clarity and purity arise thus: when one uses turns, and when, passing from one matter to another, one uses for the one a completion and for the other an announcement.

As to diction, brevity and conciseness arise when one uses not the periphrastic forms of words but the direct ones; when one does not labour over the diction by setting equivalents side by side, but, having made the matter plain by the significative word, at once gets free of it and in few words; and when one is not ambitious over the diction, but looks rather to the matters.
As to figure, chastening arises thus: when one cuts short the resultant clauses of the discourse; when one uses apologies; when one uses corrections.

A clause is a composition of two or more words, as: "I lack no pretext for which to help Nicias." A phrase is a part of a clause, set down either by itself, as: "Know yourself," and "Nothing too much"; or with others, as: "I beseech you, by your children, by your wives, by the goods you possess."

Every discourse, clearly, consists of conceptions and of delivery, which lies in diction, in figure, in rhythm. We must say, then, what it is that makes the distinctions between the political discourses and the simple ones; for the conceptions of the simple are not the same as those of the political. For if the conception is the same, yet the diction is not the same; or if the diction too is the same, yet the rhythm is not the same; or if the rhythm too is the same, yet the figure is not the same.

But when you come to the establishing of the difference and say, "For it is easier to rule oxen and sheep and every herd than men," then I say that you are leading the discourse off into simpler conceptions; for they belong to character and manner, which preserved the simplicity of the discourse. The political man, then, having set down a proposition, sets beside it the establishing points, always choosing the more political of the conceptions; for instance, to speak, in the matter of revolts, of "shepherds as rulers" is not more political; or again, "we have never yet perceived herds banding together" — a political man would not say it; but this man, in keeping with what suited him, furnished the divergence to his arguments.

And some conceptions are such that nothing is to be understood in them besides; while some are such as to have character, and the character is not one nor simple, but varied — one a graceful character, one a good character, one making manifest sweetness, one kindness, one such a character as to make manifest, of itself, much dignity, as this too: "Autolycus, then, sat beside his father." It was a thing of great dignity, and in the conception, to make the lad sit beside his father. For such conceptions are dignified; and most of all his character was preserved for him by his not using elaboration of his own — as if he had said, "Autolycus, then, sat beside his father, as a son should sit with a father" — for such a thing is political. He let, then, the character and the dignity be made manifest.

Dignity arises in the simple discourse in many other ways too, but more dignified is when you transfer from a person to the matters; for it is not the same to say of the person, "the beautiful are kings by nature" — for this is boyish — as to bring it out upon the matter, "that beauty is something kingly by nature." And for the sake of the dignity in the conception, the addition after this: "especially if one possesses it, as Autolycus did, with modesty and temperance."

Wherever you wish to work sweetness, you will use such metaphors, transferring words lying upon other matters onto others; and when you do not remain upon the precisely significant, for instance, the significative of the subject "they gave," and the transferred from the trope, "and they honoured Cheiron on account of his justice," instead of "they gave."
Juxtapositions of like things, too, work a fine and keen discourse, as in the Anabasis, of Cyrus: "he offered prizes also to the cavalry squadrons, whichever should ride best."

And it makes the discourse true to introduce something that seems to be against you, to admit it and let it stand without doing it away, for instance: "But if any of you, seeing the enemy to be fearful, has supposed . . . to me he seems to think rightly." For, in order that the other things which Cyrus went through to the soldiers should seem to be spoken truly, this he not only did not do away, but even assented to it, though it was against him.

Sometimes Xenophon, even before what he wishes to say, introduces it through the example itself; and the establishings of them are without examples, for the most part, as is plain in all the rest, but most of all in the Memorabilia; for there, in what manner he has made Socrates discoursing about each thing and demonstrating each, it is possible for one examining to learn that it has been advanced in this manner.

Yet this does not seem to me to suit the simple discourse, if indeed the discourse must appear as free of design as possible, and simple and pure; and Xenophon sets down each of the thoughts bare and separately, as in the Agesilaus, by themselves, whence one might even think the thoughts to have been flung down. Yet they have not been flung down, but each has been advanced with elaborateness, while stripped of the fine examination and addition and transposition and interchanges and all such things; and they simply appear such; whence there are also many continuous distensions, and beginnings of thoughts no longer joined, but completed; and further, the things said appear most of all as separate, one and another, and the composition is not a web, but, as it were, gathered phrase by phrase in the form of conversation.

The political men, then, take their beginnings both from the very matters and tending toward them; but Xenophon does not, in all cases, take them tending toward them, and is wont not to take them from the matters themselves, as in the Education, "A thought once came to us"; for he did not advance the discourse from the deeds of Cyrus, but argumentatively from without; on which account, going on, he made the increase little by little from without.

But the greatest of all things in the simple discourse is for the matters to proceed bare and clean, and not to mark the forces in each case; for it belongs to a political man to mark them, when you add not only the matter but also the quality — if it be great, as great; if dreadful, as dreadful — of which simplicity must have no share. At once, then, the simple writer says, "Coming forward, he said this"; but Demosthenes, "Rising up, he spoke words deserving, O Zeus and gods, of many deaths."

And among human matters too, when you bring in things that are held in honour — honouring parents, ancestors, the first founders of our customs, and exhorting others to the same — and in general the things honoured in life: these too share in dignity, such as liberty, temperance, justice, as when you call liberty, and what is achieved through it, the definition and standard of happiness. And in general one might mention countless such things, which are plain to all who have once entered upon this inquiry.

And when one proposes something monstrous to the hearers, which they would not willingly accept, as in the speech Against Aristogeiton, where, having gone through what happens in the assemblies through the inexperience of such orators, he proposed the monstrous thing with gravity: "If, then, you wish this, and these men do this with our consent, we must go on our way and let it be."

Further as to amplitude: when, in the midst of a thought or of the thoughts, before completing the sense, one throws in other thoughts — which, unless it is done in some measure, produces dreadful obscurity. An example of this kind of amplitude is in the speech Against Aristocrates: "With reason, then, men of Athens, you would both give heed to me and listen with goodwill to what I say"; then the things that establish why one must attend and listen, one thrown in upon another, and these rendered oblique: "for since I am not one of those who trouble you, nor of those who take part in your public life, I declare that I shall prove a deed of such magnitude to have been done, if you will help me with all the power that is in you and listen eagerly." And the good that is to result for them from listening is not one but two: the one from the present — "you will both save this"; the other from the future — "and you will make men not shrink, if anyone thinks that he too can do the city some good." This much, then, is filled out and nothing is wanting to it. But, that the amplitude may be greater, he set the opposite beside it and resumed. And what was the opposite of "make someone more eager to do the city some good"? "But as it is, many men who fear this — though perhaps not skilled in speaking, yet better men than the skilled — do not even bring themselves to consider any of the common affairs." And this too would have been complete; but here, again, it did not suffice him, but he added to what had been said a confirmation drawn from his own case: "I myself, at any rate, be well assured, would have shrunk even from bringing this very indictment," so that in this way the matter of "attending to the speaker" is interwoven. And: "Nor will this be absurd — that some shrink from doing the city good, as now they do shrink, through fear and inexperience of speaking; I myself, at any rate, very nearly shrank as well." How, then, do you bring the accusation? And the confirmation of this from his own case: "Because I think it a terrible thing that formerly, when I sailed as trierarch to the Hellespont, I both spoke and accused certain men whom I thought to be wronging you, but that now I should keep quiet and be silent when I see certain men contriving a thing of no advantage to the city." Does it seem to you that few thoughts have been thrown in, before the whole conception comes to its close?

To credibility belongs also the use of oaths and imprecations, for instance: "I call to witness before you all the gods and goddesses who hold the land of Attica, and Apollo the Pythian, who is the ancestral god of the city, and I pray to all these: if I should speak the truth to you — and indeed I both spoke it then and at once before the people — grant me good fortune and safety; but if it be out of enmity, or for the sake of private rivalry, make me have no profit of any good." And again: "First, men of Athens, I pray to all the gods and goddesses that as much goodwill as I continue to bear toward the city and toward you all, so much may be granted me by you in this present contest." And in the speech Against Conon: "And if I swear truly, may many good things befall me, and may I never again suffer any such thing; but if I swear falsely, may I perish utterly, I and whatever is mine or shall be mine."

And when one likens absurdly, it makes the discourse vehement, for instance: "Like a scorpion with sting upraised, darting this way and that, looking to whom he may fasten some harm and bring to ruin." And again: "For just as a knife is of no use to a cook unless it cuts, so to one who wishes that by his means harm and trouble should come upon all, the sycophant who would peddle these things is of no use." And elsewhere again: "But we are like men who have drunk mandrake or some such drug."
As to delivery, elaborateness arises when the delivery is dense and continuous, and when it is verbal rather than substantive.
As to delivery, when one uses tropes — and tropes not harsh, but subdued — and when one uses a diction that is animated.

As to delivery, thus: when one uses more common words, and those that are highly significative and most vividly make plain the matters; and when one uses narrative figures; and when one uses equivalents as little as possible — by "equivalents" he means, of course, the figurative and metaphorical that are equivalent to the proper terms — and when one uses gentler words instead of harsh ones.

As to delivery, thus: when one uses the proper word for the matters instead of the trope; and when one uses hyperboles less; and when, if ever one is compelled to use some figurative hyperbole, one apologizes for it. And in what manner this is done is easy to show.

A period is constituted out of a single clause, as: "For prosperity beyond one's deserts becomes, for the foolish, a starting-point for thinking ill"; or out of two clauses, as: "For to refuse to give something from the first is the act of men exercising judgement, but to take it away from those who have it is the act of the envious"; or out of three: "Gentlemen of the jury, chiefly because I think it expedient that the law be repealed, and then for the sake of the son of Chabrias, I agreed with these men to speak with them as best I could"; or out of more: "Those who praise your ancestors, men of Athens, seem to me to speak a gratifying speech, but not one that does service to those very men whom they extol."

One must know first, then — to put it in summary as best we may — that the differences of the political discourse from the simple are taken first from the conceptions. For the political thoughts are harsher, more distinguished and drawn from more distinguished sources, and keener, working their keenness from the fact that they are rarer and distinguished; while the simple thoughts are plain, ordinary, undistinguished, and these too drawn from undistinguished arguments. Concerning the thoughts, then — to say a few things out of many — these are they.

But where the conceptions are common, neither the diction nor the figure is the same. For when he says, "A thought once came to us," and "all those who, having attempted to play the tyrant, some of them were even very quickly overthrown, did they not pay the penalty?" and again, "but others, even if they continue ruling for however long a time" — for he did not say, "those who took the cities by force and established the strongest rule for themselves."

For some conceptions, as I said, have a character lying underneath and to be inferred — such as the aforesaid, "You are always mocking us"; while others are simple and make manifest no malice, as this too: "Some, having anointed themselves, others having bathed as well"; for this makes manifest nothing more than what happened. But where the inferences are base and grieve the discourse, you must set right the absurdity in what you introduce, not simply, but by your own additions; for instance, "At once, then, one who considered what was happening would have thought that beauty is something kingly by nature" — and his own addition: "especially if one possesses it, as Autolycus did, with modesty and temperance." For, the discourse being about beauty, one would not refrain from receiving such things toward malice.

Such interweavings, too, produce dignity, for instance, "and a boy very comely and playing the lyre and dancing very finely"; for to interweave into the same thing the diverse among these takes away the difference of the kind.

And by stating the great in a small way, and the small in a great way, you will work sweetness. To name the small in a great way, we say, furnishes sweetness to the discourse; and most marvellous is such a trope — to call a thing "a war of a dog and a beast": "First, the hounds must be of each kind, not chance ones, that they may be ready to make war upon the beast."

And the over-elaborations and the figure-makings among the simple writers are unseen. For these things the ancients are of great worth; for see how he makes a figure: "and to the cavalry ones, whichever should ride best." For it would not have been the same to say "to the cavalry," for that would quickly have made the discourse contentious, but "to the cavalry squadrons, whichever should ride best." It has been figured, then, from the plural into one and set upright, and set beside the like, "to the cavalry, whichever should ride," and "to the hoplite squadrons, whichever should be in best bodily condition."
And by introducing what is said in narratives, even if it be fictitious and small, it seems to be true; for he says it as having happened.

The examples and the things set beside them, through which you would demonstrate, must be like to what is set before you, and must share with the things spoken of, either in kind, or in strength, or in time, or in the results that follow from them, or in their idioms, or in some other likeness. And this is fine in such a kind of discourse, and most of all works the plainness, whence too an interwoven abundance arises, and the discourse, from the things circling about, appears simple, both through what is said becoming more dignified and through another making it more vivid — which last seems to be rather the work of conversation.

This, then, has produced the seeming that the things said are a narrative of the deeds of a good man; yet it does not, it seems to me, suit wholly and in everything among the simple discourses, and one must have learned this, if any other idiom of Xenophon. For this is most of all, as I think, what works the discourse simple.

He has used the beginning from the very matters in the Memorabilia, so that the discourse seems outright to be forensic, at the beginning of the first laying-down of the matters, the thought not being completed: "I have often," he says, "wondered by what arguments they persuaded the Athenians."

In many places Xenophon uses many violent and Demosthenic strokes in the conceptions, and differs only in the handling, as in the Anabasis too, stating certain reasonings about Tissaphernes, that he does not plot against the Greeks — since the person is untrustworthy in respect of being willing to plot, and he cannot establish it from judgement, he, passing over to power, confirms it: "but if, being able to do you harm, we do not do it, it is plain that we do not even wish to." What, then, is it that has made conceptions so violent simple? The manner of the handling; for, setting them beside one another from presence and privation and chopping the thoughts, he says, "whether because you are in your own land, and we in a foreign land? and whether because you abound, and we are in want?" Nothing else, then, has relaxed the thoughts but the manner of the delivery. As he has done in the Agesilaus too; for since in the conception the discourse was harsh, in the delivery it was handled toward simplicity: "if, because he became surpassingly fair and good, on this account he should not meet even with moderate praises." But how do I say this? That if the conception be such, it makes the handling harsh; for he did not say it lamenting, as Demosthenes does, "For it would be a dreadful thing, if the letters sent by Philip." But some usages are proper to the simple writers, and you could in no way transfer them into political discourse, as here too the "surpassingly he became a good man."

Such things, too, share in dignity, when you discourse upon life and death — for instance, "Death is the limit of life for all men" — or when you make distinctions and definitions of natures, for instance, "There is no race of friends and of enemies."

And when you lead the discourse into an absurdity, you have produced gravity, as in the speech Against Callicles: "For surely Callicles will not compel me to drink it down." Or when you concede to the adversary things admitted to be absurd, as in the speech Against Aristogeiton: "If Aristogeiton is simply a scoundrel and a bitter sycophant, I grant it, I concede it — to you, Philocrates, such as you are, to save your like."

But that it may become still clearer to you what kind of thing it is to throw in several thoughts in the middle, here is a very clear example in the speech On the False Embassy: "For, with a man who is mortal" — one thought, from the person — "and strong only through certain circumstances, to write that we should conclude an undying agreement of disgrace against the city" — the thing that is being done. And what comes upon it is not yet completed, but he throws in more. Again: "For how is it not shameful that publicly you should all blame what was done as a result of the peace, and be unwilling to share in the actions of the Amphictyons, and feel ill-disposed and suspicious toward Philip, as though what was done were impious and dreadful, and neither just nor to your advantage; but, when you have come into the court" — now attend to what is thrown in — "to judge the audits concerning these matters" — another thought — "having sworn an oath on behalf of the city, you should let off this man, whom you have caught in the very act of doing such things" — now the thing that completes it.

To credibility belongs also when one takes up the judgements of those who hear, upon the matters of which one speaks, as though the matters were admitted even among them — when he says, in the speech Against Aristogeiton: "But this matter has long since been judged, of old, in the nature of each man, from the very hearth." And again: "You who sit in judgement come knowing, more than we accusers, both that this man owes a debt to the treasury, and that he is registered on the Acropolis, and that it is not lawful for him to speak; so that each of you holds the rank of an accuser, and knows the rights, and has no need to be taught." And: "And if you know me to be such — for I have lived my life nowhere else."

There is vehemence also when one expresses extreme indignation, for instance: "For this admits of no excess of foulness." And again elsewhere: "For this indeed is the utmost." And again: "It lacks nothing of the extreme of outrage."
The continuous and the loose composition would befit deeds and emotions; the periodic befits displays and proems and enthymemes.

The next difference concerns the handling. For just as in the political discourse there is a certain handling, so too in the simple discourse. And the difference of the handlings is this: in the political discourse they must be manifest — for in this way the discourse is advanced in a political manner, if the hearers follow along with the points at issue; but in the simple this is not so; rather, the inquiries are sometimes hidden, and one does not even know what the speaker means to say, because the discourse resembles no set design.

I have shown you, then, that of the conceptions some are taken from judgement, while some are conceptions of every sort; and some of them are taken from distinguished sources, others from small and obscure ones. This much, then, is so for you: that the simple writers use conceptions of every sort, and it is not enough for them to use only those taken from the subject matter, but sometimes also such conceptions as another might despise, and not even approach, because they are not taken from the subject matter and happen to be undistinguished; but the simple writers do not abstain from these.

First, then, the character of the simple discourse must be such as to make manifest kindness; for kindness is a virtue of judgement, and a choice springing from the understanding and judgement, and a fairness of manners. But the character must not be signified of itself, but left in the hearers, that it may seem free of design; on this account one must not mark either the dreadful as dreadful or the fearful as fearful, but it suffices me only to say, "Tissaphernes slanders Cyrus to his brother." For it sufficed him to show, from the kindred relation, what kind of thing it is to slander brother to brother; but to consider the quality and the disposition this leaves to him. But if you advanced it contentiously, you would have said this, for instance: "A thing the most dreadful and most savage of all Tissaphernes cast into his soul"; and if you wish to raise it and to set down the very thoughts because of which the slander ought not to have come about, you will add: "revering neither the gods nor justice nor the matter as most dreadful." For the very things that one might think to belong to character among those who handle political discourses, these too can make manifest character in these cases — yet less; for the manner is one thing with them and shows something else, another with these; for there it is to hint at something or to point at something else, or even to make manifest the very opposite of what you say, but here not, since it is a mark of simplicity and a plainness of understanding. For the sake of an example, let it stand in both: Demosthenes, wishing to make manifest character, what does he say? "It would, then, be quite fitting that you should make most account of such a man, and justly name him a benefactor." But Xenophon's character — his very hand followed it; so that, clearly examining the arrangement in each of them, we should find the character.

And wherever you introduce the things about to happen, or the things happening, as already having happened, you make the discourse dignified, for instance: "And when the flute-girl had piped for them, and the boy had played the lyre."

He made a marvellous sweetness in the Agesilaus too, saying, "Whenever indeed he marched, he led the army drawn up in such a way that they could best help themselves"; then he brought on an example, as a simple man making manifest sweetness with dignity: "and quietly, as the most temperate maiden would advance." And the relaxation lies in the diminishing of the example and in its not being wholly alike; for what does a maiden resemble in an army? Nevertheless, the saying "the temperate maiden" had cheapness, but the turning round and the attending purpose belonging to the person worked dignity with sweetness, "as the most temperate maiden would."

And to say something briefly and to set beside it many things belongs to true power, for instance, "having summoned" — then whom? "Araspes" — then whence? "a Mede" — then also the ground of acquaintance: "who had been his friend from boyhood" — then another: "to whom he had given his robe."

This observation is in all the beginnings of his discourses — not to state it as though introducing a second thought, and so to separate the first, but to lay down at once the things depending on the thought and to go on at length. It is an idiom not to change the quality of the thought, and so to introduce it generically first, which a political man would have done, raising the discourse by standing — for instance, "A thought once came to us, what kind of thing the nature of the beautiful happens to be" — then so the species, "how many democracies and how many tyrannies." And another idiom is not to do it in a declarative figure, for instance, "Nothing is harder to persuade than human nature," but, as humanly as possible, with a question, he examined: "A thought once came to us." And another is not to use a diffuse but a contracted diction: "A thought once came to us" belongs to simplicity.

In general, everywhere, in as many cases as he has stated many matters loosely in the briefest compass and has completed the thought, he has spoken with good rhythm, for instance: "and when she rose up, all the women about her rose up with her." Yet one must not enclose many matters in the simple discourse, as Demosthenes did, "for if, when we came, having helped the Euboeans," but in few, that the discourse may be most easy for you to follow.

In these matters lies the greatest danger in political oratory: either to follow on and be drawn after the very nature of the conceptions, and, departing altogether from the matters at hand, to corrupt the soundness of the discourse and render it hollow, so that one becomes like the cloud-gathering sophists; or else, having considered the due measure in these things — how far the contending discourse may be raised, and with what elements, when mingled, it is not wanting — to keep dignity itself within the bounds of the contest, and not to err. So much, then, for the benefit of those who would learn.

And when, having divided up everything, one leaves some single thing to the adversary as being no less for him than against him, gravity arises, for instance: "Except, by Zeus, there is — there is a brother of his, the one who has brought this fine suit against him." And again, having done away with the reasons why it should not be so, he adds: "Except that one might say this: that they were mad — for there is nothing else to say."

Amplitude is produced also when one examines not only what is consequent, but also takes up the opposite, as in the speech On the False Embassy. The simple, consequent form would have been thus: "For since you elected this man an envoy, to guard the rest." Here, having taken up the opposite, he thus brings in the consequent: "You elected him" — first the "for what he was not to do," then "for what he was to do" — "not as one of those who would sell out your interests, nor as one of those who had put their trust in Philip" — then now the consequent — "but as one who would guard the others." And again in the speech On the False Embassy: "And when the assembly came, Aeschines, coming forward before us all" — and he did not at once bring in the consequent, "made the following report," but first, by way of the opposite of the consequent, what he ought to have reported and did not. And what were these things? "First, from making any report at all about the negotiations, or about what had been said in the Council — if indeed he disputed my speaking truly — he wholly refrained." Then now, in the consequent, what he did: "and he harangued and spoke such words as these." But, that you may know that the observations of amplitude have kinship with one another: we said above that amplitude is to take up the generic beforehand and bring in the species; but now let us also say that amplitude is to examine not only the consequent things, but also the opposites of the consequent. Here he has done both: what he did not do and what he did, setting the opposite before the consequent; and the generic things he took up before the species — the generic things he stated in: "and he spoke such words, and possessing such great and such goods, that he carried off all of you, having taken you in." This is the generic; now the species: "for he said that he had come having persuaded Philip"; then again generically: "of all things that are to the advantage of the city"; then by species: "both concerning the affairs in the Amphictyony and concerning all the rest." And in the speech Against Meidias too: "that, if anyone is outraged by this man" — the consequent — "he thinks fit to obtain justice"; the opposite of the consequent — "and does not keep silence."

To credibility belongs also to make strong asseverations about the facts, when you say: "Be well assured, men of Athens, that you have been deceived; and for what reasons you have, with good cause, suffered this, hear me." And in the speech On the False Embassy he made a strong asseveration at once: "As for convicting this man of having done many dreadful things, and of deserving the utmost penalty, I am confident and trust greatly." And in the speech Against Stephanus: "I shall prove to you that this Stephanus has both borne false witness and done so out of base greed, and is becoming his own accuser: so great is the conspicuousness of the matter."

And in general, wherever accusations are made over admittedly clear wrongdoings, because the wrongs are plain to all, the discourse attains vehemence, as in the speech Against Meidias and in the speech Against Aristogeiton. But the greatest thing one must know is this: that when the points at issue are not strong on either side, but on one side they are not plain, and yet the speaker draws the discourse together as though upon matters that are practically admitted — such is the speech Against Meidias.
Diction becomes obscure when one uses too archaic and ambiguous language, as: "O Zeus, might it fall to me to bring down the boar"; or in some other way, such as time, or cause, or place.

The figures, in the political discourse, are harsh, vehement, refutative, forceful; in the simple they are relaxed, plain, showing no refutation nor any examination, but more ordinary and sprawling. For those make the discourse intense and political, while these make it simple, being, as it were, the speech of a private man and of conversation.

Such, then, is the matter as to the handling of the conceptions; and there is still this — that the things said in establishing the point at issue should not be stated as though set forth as a proposition, but, while it is unclear toward what they are said, the discourse should so proceed; for instance, not setting down beforehand that he wishes to prove Cyrus of great worth, he brings in "A thought once came to us," and, having taken up beforehand all the preliminary establishings — from which it is hard to rule men, harder than this and that — thus he brought it in: "But indeed Cyrus ruled over very many men; Cyrus, therefore, came to be of great worth." And this is the handling of simple discourse, when what is said is not manifestly a proposition.

Xenophon works the characters, first, by looking to the idioms of the persons about whom he happens to be making his discourse; then by looking at the occasions, and besides these the circumstances and the things that have befallen and the things present to them and the things attending; from which, reasoning, he finds how to work characters in the discourses, and, by Zeus, passions too. But that one may begin from the books themselves: in the Symposium there is every virtue, and the discourse and the plainness of understanding belong to the things said, which one might thus call character; and almost the whole discourse has been advanced thus. Whence, then, did this come to him? From seeing the occasion and what kind of thing the matter is and the things attending by nature — for instance, what kind of thing a banquet is, and what things happen to be said and done at a banquet. Looking forward to these, he worked the discourse, for instance, right at the beginning of the discourse: "But to me it seems that of fair and good men not only the things done in earnest are worthy of record, but also the things in their amusements." The thought belongs to character — that one must accept also the things done in amusement by great and good men — and it is the observation of the simple, that one must not in every way pursue the distinguished and the great, but also the things that seem paltry and contemptible. Again, in the Memorabilia, having learned the idiom of Socrates's purpose, he led the discourse with an eye to this; for, the subject matter being worthy of anger and rebuke — that so worthy a man as Socrates was condemned — nevertheless this man, as a simple man, showed character here too: "I have often," he says, "wondered," and did not say, "at what one might be angry," or "at what it is worthy to rebuke." One must, however, observe this too: how, while setting down subdued words for the sake of simplicity, he nonetheless, in the proper place, made manifest the magnitude of the matter; for the "I wondered" and the "often" are no small emphasis. Again, in the Education, see how he handled it, saying, "A thought once came to us." Now the thought is, in what manner Cyrus, while a boy, was reared, and what education he shared in, and what deeds he did, and how he became the most fortunate of men; but this means something else for the man. For he has not chosen to praise Cyrus, nor does he care in what manner Cyrus was educated or reared; but since he advances the discourse in character, he has used a sketch of what kind of man the good man must be, and what nurture and what education he must use, and what kind he must be while still among children, and what kind when one becomes a youth, and what deeds and pursuits befit the fair and good man; but Cyrus is, as it were, just a name for him. In the same manner, in the Memorabilia too, he has handled such discourses; for there it is told by him, concerning many, in what manner one must bear oneself toward one's own fatherland and toward friends and in all household matters; yet it is not told hypothetically — for instance, "one must bear oneself thus and so toward friends," nor "one must bear oneself thus toward brothers," nor "there must be a display of statesmanship before one becomes a man wise and skilled in affairs" — but, supposing other persons, he teaches you in what manner one must do such things; as he speaks of Chaerephon, who was at variance with his brother: "Tell me," he said, "are you alone ignorant that one must bear oneself toward brothers thus?" — but he set forward another person. When, then, you wish to advance a discourse in character, you do not introduce it hypothetically, "one must do this or that," but, supposing another person, you say whatever you wish someone to do, that "that man was such and did these things."

And wherever you throw in dignified words, you will work, along with the dignity, a power of beauty too: "Zeus and Cheiron were brothers, of the same father, but of mother the one of Rhea, the other of a Naiad nymph." For to make it common, "of the same father," and to state the difference, "of mother the one of this, the other of that," has, along with the simplicity, dignity too.

And concerning sweetness we have spoken in what precedes too, both all that it accomplishes in the political discourse and again all in the simple. The virtue of sweetness is nearly more the property of the simple.

These things, then, seem to suffice also for advancing the discourse with power; but most of all, when you receive the truth said against you not as true, it belongs to a simple man, as Socrates too says, "You are always mocking us." He made character by the subduing of his judgement, and by not boasting at that man's praise, but attending to it as to a jest; for what that man said in earnest, this one received as though being mocked.

Let the end, both of the word and of the whole discourse, stand for you in the long form; the clauses are judged each by themselves, but let the discourse be simple, as being completed by clauses, but in the form or quality of the discourse making manifest a certain density and a novel and simple interweaving; and these are made from a single word, for instance, "A thought once came to us," instead of "we once considered." For the keen brevity makes simplicity, so that, the observation being changed, it comes about that from simplicity there is harshness or standing, and the source from which standing arises is its being something gentle.

To use words unemphatically works cheapness. Wherefore the simple discourse is in danger of coming round to cheapness, coming very near to it through using such words too. It is possible, then, to escape and to avoid cheapness by the juxtaposition of equivalents, for instance: "And when Darius fell sick and suspected the end of his life." And to use, by metaphor, words lying upon other matters belongs to the simple writers, for instance, "he made many lovers of his own friendship," and again, "the attendants of the Greeks"; for he did not shrink from naming the rearmost of the Greeks "attendants"; and the use of the same word, "they were persuading, we were persuaded"; and, chopping the thoughts, "we sent envoys"; for to advance the things loose from one another makes the discourse simple and makes manifest a certain character, as of one speaking the things that happened with speed. And all the names of places and regions that are fit in simple discourse, these one must choose, and further those having less force and less esteemed, for instance, "gymnasia, hippodromes," and when indeed you set them beside one another, choosing, "gymnasia of men exercising, hippodromes of horsemen riding" — all these belong to simplicity. And the words in the simple discourse must not be advanced upon one matter alone, but must signify two and three, for instance, since "going away" has several species, all these must be considered; for it comprises in itself both the near and the far, both on land and on sea, both having trouble and giving trouble, and, in general, there are countless things it signifies. And such words, in which it is possible to speak of barley and meal and oil, seem rather to make simplicity in the discourse; for the discourse is about less distinguished things. But a political man would shrink from approaching such words; and wherever he does approach them, one must know well that it will be either for the sake of vividness or so that character may arise in the discourse. The rhythm, being different, rescues the matters, and the unlikeness of the political discourse is no longer about the conceptions, but about the delivery; for the perfected and wholly complete political discourse must be such both in conception and in delivery. But sometimes the conception is simple, while the delivery is political, as in the speech Against Callicles too Demosthenes says, "that barley was wetted, and that, drying it, she saw not even three medimni of it, and of meal about half a medimnus; and that a jar of oil was tipped over, but that, nevertheless, no harm was done." And this too with dignity, where the proper term, if stated, would be in danger of making cheapness, as if you said, "yet that it was not poured out"; here he, instead of the proper and the specific, changing into the generic, said, "yet that no harm was done." And to interweave through the same words seems to belong to simple discourse, but it relaxes the intensity of the political discourse, as in the speech On the False Embassy too Demosthenes says, "For who does not know that by the Phocian war and by the Phocians being masters of Thermopylae . . ." — yet this security from the place and the matters he brought on aggressively, as in a completion.

Now let us return to the sources from which the less dangerous kind of dignity is constituted. These are illustrious deeds and reflections, and the rarest and most extraordinary of actions — for instance, that Xerxes conceived the idea of yoking the Hellespont and cutting through Athos and sailing across it; that the Athenians endured to abandon their city and embark upon their ships; that the Lacedaemonians shut their gates against the King. For these are great things, works and reflections of dignity, and they naturally raise the discourse, too, into dignity.

And when you bring the renowned dead into the judgement, such a thing seems grave, for instance: "Yet how greatly would our ancestors groan!" And again: "Yet what wrath, do you think, or what verdict would your ancestors have set against the authors of this ruin?"

To amplitude belongs also not to bring in the thoughts — that is, the facts — bare, but to take up along with them the disposition behind such things, or the quality of that disposition. In this way he produced amplitude: "The Lacedaemonians seem to me to be doing the work of very clever men"; then the thing done by them: "for now they say the Eleans must recover certain parts of Triphylia." And in the Philippics: "You would, it seems to me, deliberate far better about the war and the whole preparation"; then he adds the reason these things were taken up beforehand: "if you would consider, men of Athens, the situation of the country against which you are making war."

Credible also is this: when one greatly slanders, as dreadful and grievous, the very things from which one wishes to seem most far removed, for instance: "For having accused me of things that anyone in his right mind would shrink even from saying — that I killed my own father." And in the speech Against Meidias: "For to the wretched and miserable man, when a dread and grievous charge had befallen him." And again: "He made neither gods nor sanctity a hindrance to such a speech, nor did he shrink, nor was he ashamed before the very men to whom he spoke."

Diction is redundant if it has a word doubled without need, as: "I said, I spoke, I declared"; and if, concerning things already mentioned which we have stated, we should state the same things again afterward as well.

Nor, indeed, is the diction the same for them, but there is a certain difference in the diction too. For in the political discourse, sometimes the thought is completed, sometimes it must be joined to another thought; for the discourse must be advanced with all security and intensity. In the simple it is not so; rather the diction seems to be advanced as it chances, showing a slackness and no studied care of the diction. Further, in the political discourse, whatever one wishes to signify, this very thing and this alone must be made manifest by the diction; in the simple, the single word sometimes signifies one thing, and two, and three. And in diction the beauties are produced by the juxtaposition of words, for instance, "a keeper of horses, of horses," "a keeper of swine, of swine."

Often, too, the thoughts must not all be strong, as the thoughts of political discourses are, but some must be set down in a subdued way, and seeming to be the weaker; and some, if possible, such as would appear even ridiculous — as also in the Symposium, right at the beginning of the discourse, he says: "But to me it seems that of fair and good men not only the things done in earnest are worthy of record, but also the things done in their amusements." The thought belongs to character — that one must accept also the things done in amusement by fair and good men. And this is the observation of the simple discourse — that one must not in every way pursue the distinguished and the great, but also the things that seem paltry and contemptible.

It is possible not only to seem to furnish the form of character in discourse by the plainness of understanding, but also by its opposite — for instance, to clothe a discourse with something harsher and more austere, when such a thing is supposed; and again, if one should clothe a lover with words proper to him, and likewise in all cases with an eye to the passions, in the manner in which, in the Education too, he worked passions from the surrounding circumstances — all that is said about Abradatas and his wife. But the whole virtue is to guard and preserve the idioms of each, just as they were. Thus he has made Cyaxares irascible throughout, and another man having some idiom in his soul; for these things work great characters in the discourse. And you would guard this, if you follow the previous understanding and the purpose of the discourse, considering what it means and looking to the idiom of him about whom you are speaking.

And to say something generically is more dignified than by species, for instance, generically, "lest he suffer something"; for it is not the same to say by species, "lest he be pierced through, lest he be slaughtered." And to gather all these together generically in one word, "lest he suffer something."

In general, as the matters came about, so one must take the beginnings, for instance: "To Darius and Parysatis are born two sons"; for here, even if the theme is great, yet the beginning is from certain bare matters.

And to anticipate the judgement belongs to simplicity, for instance, "knowing well," and "thinking," and "considering." And it is fine too to lay down the thoughts and to introduce them as from another's judgement. And Xenophon uses this most of all in the Education, saying every time, "But if any of you thinks this . . ."

For the sake of an example, let there be a thought that of itself, by its very conception, partakes of dignity: "No, by our ancestors who faced the first danger at Marathon and who stood in the line at Plataea." For here the question at issue was whether the city did right or wrong to risk the battle at Chaeronea, whether it was a mistake to choose this war or not. This is the point at issue, and the demonstration was that it was not a mistake, since our ancestors who faced the first danger at Marathon did not err either. But to swear, as though by gods, by our ancestors — this carries the utmost height of dignity: "No, by our ancestors who faced the first danger at Marathon." And it is plain that the occasion for such conceptions is in distinguished and superlative contests, not when we are judging someone, or being judged, over a matter of damages or some other paltry affair. One might also say that the whole thing is a figure; for the very words "No, by our ancestors who faced the first danger at Marathon" are not an oath, but an illustration, as if to say: "You have not erred in undertaking the danger for the freedom and safety of all, any more than those who faced the first danger at Marathon erred." For to undertake the danger for the safety of all is like facing the first danger at Marathon. The fact, then, he has shaped into an illustration instead of stating it directly, transforming it — for the sake of both brilliance and credibility together — into the semblance of an oath.

To gravity belongs also leaving things that no one would say as though they were going to be said: "We shall say, by Zeus, to the Greeks, 'There is a law of Timocrates among us; wait, then, for the ninth prytany; and then we shall come out.'"

You produce amplitude also when, before stating what is being introduced, you take up beforehand its confirmation, for instance in the speech Against Leptines. If he had spoken simply and without amplitude, he would have said thus: "and of those who bade those from the city repay, and of those who bade them jointly discharge it." But now see how he took up the confirmations beforehand in each case: of the one party he did not at once say "those from the city," but in the middle, "of those who bade the borrowers repay — those from the city"; and of the other party he did not at once set the antithesis, "to discharge it jointly," but again took up beforehand the confirmation: "of those who thought fit that this should be the first sign — to discharge the money jointly."

Credible also is to anticipate the assessment and to fix penalties against oneself for the things one is treating of, for instance: "I, sailing as a volunteer, am ready to suffer anything." And again elsewhere, in the Philippics: "Neither now nor hereafter give heed to me as one in his right mind."

Diction is idle when it consists of barbarous words, newly coined and counterfeit; on which account it appears unseasonable, assigning the words of some things unseasonably to others and not expressing the matters. And indeed, if discourse had been devised for any purpose other than persuasion, there might perhaps have been some dispute; but since it is quite plain that the whole disposition of the faculty of reason has been set toward this one end, it must, surely, be one of two things: either the discourse is not right, nor appears sufficient, or else it is both best and prevails over its hearers. And discourse is a token of common humanity and of goodwill toward all, not of bitterness or of misanthropy.

And concerning the rhythms we likewise say that there is a certain difference between the political discourse and the simple; and in general the difference of simplicity from the political discourse is that it belongs to simplicity for the discourse to proceed plainly, and for the hearing to be drawn along always upon what is uniform, and for there to be nowhere any checks in the discourse, nor any obstacle anywhere to the hearing. But where, as the discourse proceeds, a turning-back has occurred, and something has, as it were, met the hearing as an obstacle from the check produced by the turning-back, there the figure is contentious, and the discourse has by its rhythm already become more political; for such things always turn the hearer about and do not allow him simply to follow along — which last is the work of simplicity.

As to delivery, then, neither of the two conceptions is harshly stated — neither the "A thought once came to us," nor the "But to me it seems." For since what was said in the Symposium seemed undistinguished — to recount the things done in amusements — and no political man would have done this, it being undistinguished, he advanced it with an apology, "But to me it seems." But if the discourse had begun for him with a declarative word, such as "It seems to me," the discourse would have become harsher and would have seemed more to belong to Critias or some such man.

The characters, in simple discourses, take on intensity and dignity, when one, making manifest one's own judgement, leaves the character in the conception alone — for instance, if you said, marking it, "The gods gave and honoured Cheiron, as was right, having admired him for being just and for having done the deeds of beauty, because he was just and practised the rest of virtue"; for in these you make manifest your own judgement, how you stand toward such men; but for Xenophon it sufficed only to keep silent upon the conception: "and Cheiron, on account of his justice," and so on.

Amplitude arises in the simple discourse too, when one, having made a thought oblique, throws in another, a second, the understanding not yet completed nor the conclusion brought on, so that it seems one conception; for instance, "And while the Lacedaemonians were deliberating about these things, Agesilaus undertook" — now the completing part, "to cross over," no longer made oblique; for it would have become long, for instance, "having crossed, to do this and that," but "to cross over."

And not to be astounded at the things at which one might be astounded, and not to wonder at things worthy of wonder, but simply to state what has happened without marking it of oneself — this too belongs to simplicity.

The recounting of antiquity, too, belongs to dignity, as: "But considering that Orestes, who had slain his mother, escaped by obtaining merciful gods for his judges." In this way, then, dignity may arise as to thought.
To concede past absurdities, too, is gravity, as: "Let this, then, be settled between us up to this point."

This too belongs to amplitude: when you do not state what is being introduced bare, for instance in the speech Against Leptines.
