The thing introduced is: "that the gifts the people has given be valid, being in accordance with the standing laws." But he took up beforehand the quality of the thing introduced: "this, which already exists among the standing laws"; then the quality taken on: "a fine thing, men of Athens, and a clear one"; and now the thing introduced: "that the gifts the people has given be valid." And again, upon this, the verdict: "Just it is, O Earth and gods!" And in general, wherever you do not introduce the facts bare, but take up something of them beforehand or add something to them, you will produce amplitude.

To credibility belongs also assigning more against oneself than the truth, for instance: "Of the foreigners there are exempt persons; I will set them at ten — though, by the gods, as I said just now, I do not think there are five. But of the citizens, again, there are not five or six. Of both, then, sixteen. Let us make them twenty; or, if you wish, thirty."

As Xenophon in the Symposium — for now I shall set out their examples too for you, that the observations of simplicity may become clearer to you: "Women, at any rate, especially if they happen to be brides, like the wife of this Niceratus here and of Critobulus, have no need of perfume." And the turning-back: "for they themselves smell of it." This, then, one must understand thus: that these women have no need of perfume from a man, for they have it from themselves, being brides. It is worth observing the matter of the turning-back; for it belonged to simplicity to go on as far as "they have no need of perfume," but the giving of the cause, set beside it by way of the turning-back, made the discourse exceedingly nimble — "for they themselves smell of it" — and the discourse comes near to having become political by its rhythm.

As to figure, by a relaxed figure; for he would not have done it with strain, as one of the political writers would have said: "I do not hold the same opinion as the many about earnest men; for the many think nothing else of theirs worthy of record but the things done in earnest, whereas with me it is not so; but no less do the things done in amusements seem worthy of remembrance than what they might do in earnest." He did not advance it thus, but with a relaxed and altered figure, "But to me it seems"; then, in keeping with the idiom of the discourse, things belonging to character, and the words "fair and good men." And again he says, "And when the horse-race ended." The figure seems to be relaxed and sprawling; but a political man would not have done it thus, but more intensely: "Just when the horse-race ended," or in some such manner.

It belongs to the man's idiom, and to all the simple writers, to furnish, as much as possible, a kind character too, yet not to signify this very thing of itself. And consider from here the character of simplicity: whether it does not seem to you to belong to a kind man, that one about to die should wish both his children to be present with him: "And so kind and affectionate was Darius, that he wished both his children to be present with him. And when Darius fell sick and suspected the end of his life, he wished both his sons to be present with him." This belongs to kind character; for it has shown you a fatherly disposition, and it is the virtue of judgement, and the character of a simple man, such as would be kind. He made a kind character in the Symposium too, in the case of the woman displaying marvels, saying, "so that those watching were afraid." Here too, then, the character appeared kind — that the watchers were afraid at the strangeness of the spectacle.

Every amplitude works a power in the discourse, but we must consider in what respect the power that arises in the simple discourse differs from the political. Consider, then: "For prosperity beyond one's deserts becomes, for the foolish, a starting-point for thinking ill." I say, then, that the declarative form of the figure is not profitable in the simple; for it clothes it with standing and power, but it is no longer simple nor according to a man — that one should so state the matter — but lofty and puffed up; nor the subordinating particle, the "for"; for such particles compel the discourse, enclosing the thoughts, to become rounded and hard and squeezed tight; whence one must not add the particles, whenever we wish to bring out some sign of power, but to begin simply from verbal forms.

And to begin even from the nominative case makes the discourse simple, and to break the thoughts up phrase by phrase. Often the simple writers use also conceptions brought in from without, beside the subject matter, for instance, "We have never yet perceived the herds banding together against the shepherd." The political men too use conceptions from without, such as histories or examples, but they tend them with announcements or justifications.

To gravity belongs also the deprecating of absurd things: "Yet may the affairs of the city not come to this, men of Athens." And: "It is ten thousand times better to die than to do anything out of flattery for Philip."

You produce amplitude also when, introducing something of your own — for instance, "Conon did you such great services" — you do not at once say what he did, but, taking up beforehand from what state and how things stood when he did it, as in the speech Against Leptines. The benefaction is "he won a sea-battle," but before saying this he took up and led on beforehand both the manner and the circumstances of what he did: "after the people's return from the Piraeus, when our city was weak and possessed not a single ship, being himself a general in the King's service and having received not the slightest resource from us"; now the thing he did: "he defeated the Lacedaemonians at sea."

To credibility belongs also showing that, though the matters one undertakes are difficult, one speaks them because it is to the city's advantage that they be spoken, even if one runs some risk oneself, having chosen — should it be needful even to suffer something — to do so for the common good. An example of this is in the deliberative speeches: "I see, indeed, how difficult it is to speak what is best; for since you have been deceived, and some have chosen this course, others that, if anyone undertakes to speak the contrary, and you will not wait to learn, he will gratify neither party and will be misrepresented to both. Nevertheless, I shall choose rather, if indeed I am to suffer this, to seem to be talking nonsense, than, contrary to what I think best, to leave you to be deceived by certain men."

The ancient writers, both the simple and the political men, use the figures in varied ways; for the very things that, in political discourse, make the discourse keen, here produce simplicity. And the rhythm of delivery must be such as to advance and step forward rather than to press on as though bearing down upon itself, not as in the political writers, where they set beside the matter the qualities, when they say either "the most dreadful of all things," or "that at which you will all be indignant," or "for this is a monstrous thing." For before stating the matter the political writers show the quality, sometimes before the matters, sometimes bringing it on after the matters. And this too belongs to good rhythm: "Yet a man who at that time, in the foremost city, was judged by the best men worthy of the fairest prize — what further proofs does he need of his excellence even before he came to rule?" This too seems to me to have wrought good rhythm in the discourse; and what works the good rhythm is this — to have enfolded the thoughts and, having completed it, to set the thought at rest, so that what is said after it is no longer joined to it, but seems to be the beginning of another discourse. For what does he say? "But all that came about when he was already among men." Xenophon does not use this figure in many places; for it is harsher and more forensic, and we are accustomed to bring on such things with proven matters, either as men forcing the point or as those who seem to be saying something with great emphasis. Still, as for its other good rhythm, this too has come about marvellously — that the continuous distensions have been made in a single breath of discourse: "yet at that time," "in the foremost city," "judged by the best men," "deemed worthy of the fairest prize"; and the saying of many thoughts, one by one, toward a single phrase, belongs to power and rhythm.

Another character again, unseen and hidden, as befits the simple discourses: "Cyrus, then, goes up, having taken Tissaphernes as a friend." For why need one declare and say, "having taken Tissaphernes, the man most plotting against him, as a friend"? But to conceal it and let it pass by itself — this has the character. And attend to this most of all, that the simple writers do not mark the forces, but think it right that they should be shown of themselves, unless somewhere a fitting occasion appear, as in the Cynegeticus: "I, then, exhort the young not to despise hunting." He had here an occasion and a marvellous character, after results so great, to use it hypothetically too, from his own person: "I, then, exhort." And when you say the opposite of the significant and relax the emphasis, you work character; for you do not say, "to hold to hunting and to be in earnest about hunting," but the opposite, "not to despise hunting nor the rest of education." And this does not allow the discourse to become cheap, when you set a distinguished thing beside one not seeming very distinguished, "not to despise hunting nor the rest of education." To interweave, then, the greater with the smaller, and to mix in something generic with what is stated by species, belongs to a man of knowledge; for from these come men good for war and for other things: "This, then, one must do, for this reason." The justification, then, is common to both the political and the simple; but the figures differ — to say it without interweaving, "not only for war, but also for other things."

To amplitude belongs also that which both makes the discourse distinguished and gives it standing — when one does not introduce the matters by themselves and name them upon the subject, for instance, "Callias appeared worthy to behold through being possessed by love of Autolycus," but takes on from without certain definite things along with the indefinite: "All, then, who are possessed by some one of the gods seem worthy to behold." And if, then, you wished to pass quickly to the subject and not to raise the discourse very much, you would have said, "but most of all those possessed by love"; but as it is, it was raised much more through the differences being taken up beforehand in the middle, before the subject is led on: "but those possessed by other things seem to be seen as more terrible and to speak more fearfully and to be more vehement."

Interchanges, too, suit the simple discourse, for instance, "he acknowledges, not acknowledging"; and to begin from the same words belongs to simplicity. To simplicity belongs also not to use harsh but subdued terms. For it belongs to harshness to say, "this privately, this publicly"; but the simple writer says, "at home" and "at the altars." And the use of such prepositions, for instance, "for it had been noised abroad," is simple.

Credible also is to state beforehand the very thing that another, opposing you, might say, for instance in the speech On the Symmories. The point at issue is that one must oppose those who advise war against the King; but since the objection came from that quarter — "Are we, then, not to make war upon the common enemy and barbarian?" — for this reason he credibly took up beforehand what one might say from that side against the King, and says it himself: "I consider the King the common enemy of all the Greeks"; then what he now himself proposes: "yet I would not, on this account, advise the others to take up war against him."

The simple writers delight also in the words, transferring them from one thing to another, as Xenophon too in the Agesilaus says, "he made many lovers of his own friendship"; for "lover" seems to be the word of something else. And again, "but they themselves, catching sight of the attendants of the Greeks." Here again he used a word lesser than the matter; for the word "attendants" is more wont to be said of slaves, but he did not shrink from naming the followers and the rearmost of the camp "attendants." And in the Memorabilia: "I wonder, then," he says, "how on earth the Athenians were persuaded that Socrates was not sound concerning the gods." He transferred it here as something proper to the kind of discourse.

He made character again, with sweetness, saying in the Memorabilia, "and that he should not think he has the greatest gain in having acquired a good friend"; he made a sweet character by naming the matter from the lesser. For instead of saying that the substances of friends all become his, and the helps in life, he, by this one word, which makes manifest both sweetness and character, says, "having acquired a good friend."

It is much more in the historical manner to set the figures upright and not to make them oblique; and to make them oblique belongs to the political men; for it has dignity and amplitude. If, then, you made it oblique, you would say thus: "the horse-race having ended"; but to set it upright is of this kind: "and when the horse-race ended"; but this seems relaxed and sprawling. And the political man would not have done it thus, but more intensely: "and when the horse-race ended." And as the political man is drawn together and gathers up the thoughts, so the simple man is supine and stretched out.

And optatives seem to belong rather to simplicity, such as "that he might be worthy," and "if they were pious," and "as Socrates would say," and such things; and in the Anabasis, "that they might be competent to make war," and what follows in the same figure, "and might be well-disposed toward him." Optatives make the discourse pure.

To credibility belongs also confirming from hearsay whatever you cannot establish from elsewhere: "I heard from certain people that they would no longer grant him even the harbours and markets to enjoy." And again: "As I heard from one of those who had been in the country itself, a man by no means capable of lying." But it is more credible to be able to refer it to the very hearers, for instance: "Having heard it from you, I am able to instruct you." And again: "the things I have myself heard from you, the older men."

One must, however, observe this too: how, while setting down subdued words for the sake of simplicity, he nonetheless, in the proper manner, makes manifest the magnitude of the matter, as he says at the beginning of the discourse: "I have often wondered by what arguments those who indicted Socrates persuaded the Athenians that he deserved death at the city's hands; for the indictment against him was something like this: 'Socrates does wrong, in not acknowledging the gods the city acknowledges, and in bringing in other things, and in corrupting the young.'" For the "I wondered" and the "often" are no small emphasis, and the things brought against him made it plain as well. A political man, then, would have stated both forces not once but many times; but he, having stated the simple force, was content.

And to make the rebukes by way of the denial of the opposite produces character; for instance, where the consequent would be to say "he took care," "he did not neglect," and "he blamed those who neglected," he says "he did not praise," for instance: "and indeed of the body he himself did not neglect it, nor did he praise those who neglected."

Amplitude is this too, as in the Symposium Socrates also said: "in many other cases it is plain, and in those in which the girl . . ." He spoke in an enfolding way; and what made the amplitude? The taking up of the indefinite and the passing over to something definite: "in many other cases, but it is plain also in those in which the girl . . ." And the manner is Socratic and ancient — to introduce something useful out of everything, since indeed from the beginning, until discourses about virtue were discovered, there was even the greatest doctrine, that the virtue of men and of women is the same.

And not to hasten the intensity of the delivery, but to slow it and to proceed at leisure, belongs to simplicity, for instance, "But indeed one could not blame them for these things either." And as for the results, the political men are wont rather to examine according to the results of absurd things, and this works harshness for them; but the simple writers rather according to the issues of good things, for instance, "for this, then, from no other source of rule . . ."

To credibility belongs also adding a further falsehood, for instance in the speech On the Crown, where he says that Aeschines became an Athenian late — "For late, late, I say" — then credibly he added a further falsehood: "yesterday, then, or the day before, both an Athenian and an orator." And again in the speech Against Aeschines, the truth is "he has done away with one of those who came to the audits," but the sequel he added falsely, for instance: "and the rest he threatens, going about."

Thus the conceptions are sometimes the same, but the handling makes the difference of the discourse. And you see here too the simplicity of the words. For though the subject matter is worthy of anger and rebuke — for its quality is such, that so worthy a man as Socrates was condemned — nevertheless so simple a man often says, "I wondered." And he did not say, "at what one might be angry," or "at what it is worthy to rebuke." For in simple discourse there is neither force nor passion nor vehemence, nor is the disposition of the matters of such a kind, nor such as to mark the nature of what is brought on; and by this most of all the form of the simple discourse is characterized.

A good and Socratic character is not to lead from the necessary to the necessary, for instance, "but he himself discoursed about human affairs, considering what is pious, what impious"; then from the neutral to the nominal: "what temperance, what madness, what courage, what cowardice, what a city, what a statesman." And in the same he made beauty too by chopping it short matter by matter.

And not to strain overmuch, either in the matters or in the thoughts, belongs to simplicity, and such transitions, "but indeed," "as indeed." And not to use one's own verdict, when something is worthy of praise, but the common one, is very simple, for instance, "at once the many admired him." Here there is also another source: not to say by hyperbole, "all admired," but in a subdued way, "the many admired." And it is proper to the simple writers to omit the establishing points and to state the less establishing ones, for instance, "one must have hopes of safety in being conscious to oneself of nothing — neither impiety toward the gods nor wrong toward men."

To credibility belongs also to say something as though recalling it, for instance: "I nearly passed over the very thing I most needed to say to you." And of the same manner is to say something as though searching for it: "Take now the decree too that was passed for Chabrias. Look and see; for it must be here somewhere." For to introduce something not as prepared, but as though searching for it on the spur of the moment, is like improvisation and makes the discourse credible.

It is good, too, in matters one knows, to speak as though searching for something. "By what arguments?" — for he did not say, "not by accusations nor by slanders," which would have suited a political man, but "by what arguments they persuaded the Athenians." And to speak generically, not by species: not "Anytus and Meletus," but "those who indicted Socrates." And interchanges suit the simple discourse: "he does wrong, indeed, but he does wrong."
Ironies, too, work characters — for instance, all the cases in which he has made Socrates conversing and instructing the young, as though he himself did not know, but were searching out rather.

And to set the words parallel and interwoven with one another, gaining no working, belongs to simplicity, for instance, "both to Ionians and to Aeolians and to Hellespontines." And not to abstain from things having less force and less esteemed, but to say "marketplace" and "in the marketplace," and by species "smiths, leather-workers," and such things, belongs to simplicity. Often, when the difference is greater, you interweave thus too: "yet there are some who even revolted"; and sometimes you said the thing alone and bare, sometimes you set beside it the cause, for instance, "reaching after freedom." And to take, instead of the demonstrative, the examining, belongs to simplicity, for instance, the demonstrative having vividness, "for that man, ruling very many cities on the mainland, and ruling islands too." Vividness arises sometimes in simplicity too, for instance, "Philammon, not because . . . Glaucus the Carystian."

Above all things, to credibility belong both marking the things introduced and using hyperboles. Marking, when you say: "The thing I think you must most of all guard against, men of Athens, this I still wish to say." This is when what is being introduced is governed by what has been said before. And the hyperbole in the sequel, for instance: "For if anyone shall concede that everything Leptines will say about the law, instructing you that it is well laid down, is true, yet one shameful thing — which could not be done away with whatever happened — will result for the city through the law becoming valid."

Then, of what follows, the proofs are most political; for he shows, it seems, a contradiction against the things attaching to him: "But this too seems marvellous to me — that some were persuaded that Socrates corrupted the young." But he, not setting down a proposition, thus brings on the establishing points, but simply goes through the matters, first. And one must observe the handling of the establishing points; for a political man would have stated the generic, choosing it: "how he was temperate, how self-controlled, how he held out against all toils"; but he states the species: "he was self-controlled, he says, in belly and in the pleasures of love; and how he bore himself toward winter and summer"; then he mixed the great with the small: "How, then, could he have made men impious or lawless or gluttonous?"

Some words, even apart from the matters, work character in discourses, for instance: "It is a fine thing that I have met with you." Here nothing else worked the character but the diction, "It is a fine thing that I have met with you."

It is simple too not to establish, as in a proposition, that a thing is fine, but, as in a comparison, finer than another fine thing. And to say, having stated something by way of denial, the hyperbole instead of the negation, for instance, "not even if I should." And to say, instead of the consequent, the opposite by way of denial, is simpler and more elaborate, for instance, here, "he took care," where the consequent would have been "he did not neglect."

Credible also is to concede and assent to some of the antitheses which the adversaries seem to advance against us, as in the speech Against Meidias the antithesis from their side: "Perhaps now he will say such things as that everything I say is premeditated"; then his own concession, with hyperbole: "I do indeed admit that I have considered the matter and rehearsed it as much as ever I could."

Often the simple writers use also conceptions brought in from without, beside the subject matter, such as: "We have never yet perceived the herds banding together against the shepherd," and all such things. It does not suit a political man; for even if the political men do use certain conceptions from without — such as if one should speak from examples or from histories or from some other such mode — yet at least one must use those attached to the matter, whence they are wont to tend such things either with justifications or with announcements; for instance, one out of many: "That you may know, then, that it is not even in keeping with the character of the city to make such a law valid" — then there follows talk of "money." But in the simple, the conceptions brought in are from nearly everything in life. And the things added from without produce magnitude in the discourse, when there is a distinguished name or place.

And comparative figures very much belong to simplicity and belong rather to the historical kind of discourse, but they too furnish character, for instance, "rather to these, as to generals and cavalry-commanders and seekers of office." But if you, gathering the opposite, said, "as for all who are said to be such as men see surpassing others somewhat in offices and honours and such powers, they do not seem to me to act rightly," such a manner would seem to belong rather to Critias or one of the ancient sophists.

And asyndeta belong to the simple; for they loosen the rhythm. This is opposite to the political, but suited to the simple, for instance, "Athenians, Thebans, Argives, Corinthians." It is simple too not to speak in a mass; for to speak in a mass is to say "the Persians," but partitively, "the things of the Persians."

One must observe, then, in everything, that the rhythms and the figures and the words be suited to the simple discourse, and the rhythmically uniform among the thoughts, such as "things said, things done, things deliberated"; and one must know all the figures that suit these, and everywhere preserve the simplicity that is in them.

I say, then, that the simple man uses also an unemphatic diction and figure and rhythm, as it is here too: "And when Darius fell sick and suspected the end of his life, he wished both his children to be present with him"; for the rhythm is not such as would belong to a political man, drawn together and gathering up the thoughts. The thoughts set upright have keenness instead of being made oblique; for to make it oblique would have been, "and Darius being sick." And simplicity comes near to approaching cheapness, through using most words unemphatically, as here too the "fell sick" was a bare word. On this account an equivalent was set beside it, that it might escape cheapness: "And when Darius fell sick and suspected the end of his life."

[And to speak about the matters, leaning upon others' opinions, belongs to the simple, for instance, "since they fell into faction." But when you say, "and since they fell into faction," it makes the discourse harsh.] And often, changing the cases, to use the same word, turning it about, belongs to simplicity. This, then, is of the same manner — not to conceal either the matter or the name, and to state it unseen, for instance, "he said to Cyrus." But it belongs to the historical, if a perfect discourse is needed, to bring an indefinite upon the words stated by species, for instance, "to Gorgias and Prodicus and many others." And when the thought is completed from a single completing word and stands at the end upon one word — as here, "and when he was quite plainly vexed, unless they should follow, they followed along" — it is historical and belongs to a discourse having character. And things stated singly, for instance, "all bronze, all palm-wood," belong to simplicity; but the speaking in the plural belongs to amplitude and to standing.

We say that in many places there are observations common to both the simple and the political — for instance, the marking of matters of which you are about to speak, and the considering of their nature and of what opposes what is being said by you, namely, that you are discoursing about small and paltry things. And such a thing too belongs to the simple: "Philip the jester came in," and "he wept," and that "those reclining at the banquet laughed," and that "the Syracusan presented marvels." For all these are common to both the political and the simple. But the handling of what is introduced is proper to the man; since even the announcement here is common: "I wish to make plain the things I came to know by being present." But what comes after the announcement is no longer common, but novel; for, having announced, he did not state the consequent of the announcement, but one of the things about him; for the things at which he was present were the things that took place at Callias's house; but he does not say these things at once, but the beginning from which these things began to come about, and such a thing seems to be a narrative rather.

Interweavings belong rather to the contentious writers, but could arise sometimes even in simple discourse, when the beginning is contracted, on account of the interweaving, but what follows is loose, for instance, "he was burning and ravaging." Keenness too is produced by the repetition of the interweaving, "at once he was burning, and at once he made it plain by proclamation, not proclaiming throughout nor bidding to proclaim."

It suffices, in the simple discourse too, not only to state the things that happened, but also to state them as they happened to come about, for instance, "Philip the jester, knocking at the door." The "knocking at the door" has been guarded, in that it is said not only "rapping" but "knocking"; some, however, do not think so; but that it is Greek, one need not dispute. But you, if you wished to amplify the discourse politically, would have set beside them the forces too: "Philip was a jester, who arrives suddenly, and since he found no one near him, he first resolved to leap in, but it seemed good to him to signal to another, and, coming up, he was rapping at the door."

To state some of the matters leaning upon the opinions of others belongs to the simple, for instance, "as is said." But it belongs to a political man to introduce most things from himself, for instance, Thucydides seems to have spoken simply, "having fallen into faction with one another for many years, as is said"; but if he should say, "and since they fell into faction," he makes the discourse harsh.

Some things are fine for the simple but lowly for the political, for instance, "living a hare's life"; for this is said in mockery, but it has its place; for the discourse is advanced in one way in simplicity, in another in cheapness. When, then, you wish to mock something, introduce it chopping it one by one, as Demosthenes does, "leader and chief and ivy-bearer." It is fitting, in elaborateness and in dialogue, that simplicity be mixed in the discourse with the beginnings of standing. And ending into the same, yet set apart, that it may not destroy the discourse, makes simplicity.

It is very fine, in the simple discourses, to make the fictions, and it has marvellous vividness, for instance: you, if you wished to state it as a fiction, would have said, "he himself came up and said that he had met them in good time"; but Xenophon, "It is a fine thing that I have met with you." For both to chop and to make beginnings belongs to simplicity. And in such things, when you vary it and, completing it, lead the discourse on into many beginnings, it seems to belong to the novel and the more delicate form, for instance, here: "There was beside the road the spring called Midas's, of the king of the Phrygians"; then another beginning, "at this Midas hunted the satyr"; and another beginning, the manner of the hunting, "he mixed it with wine." Such beginnings, then, and the setting of the discourse continuously upright in this way, belong to the more delicate form. But it belongs to the more ancient manner to go through the whole in a single course of the discourse: "There was beside the road a spring called Midas's, of the king of the Phrygians, at which Midas is said to have hunted the satyr; and the manner how? having mixed it with wine"; for from a single beginning to a single end the discourse has been brought to a close. And this belongs to Xenophon's mould. Concerning obscure things I have often said that one must speak as though from hearsay. And this suits the simple discourse too, for instance, "it was said," and "it was said that he gave Cyrus much money." Concerning the mythical, not that it happened, but that it is said to have happened. We have said that novelties too belong to simplicity; it is not the worse, then, to use an example here as well, as in the Anabasis Xenophon says, of Cyrus, "he sacrificed the Lycaea." This is very novel and a special construction, "he sacrificed the Lycaea." For he has used the name of the festival as if of the very thing sacrificed, stating the thing done in terms of that in which it is done and on account of which it is done; for to say "to sacrifice at the Lycaea" is customary, but "to sacrifice the Lycaea" belongs to novelty — as if you should say, "he sacrificed the Panathenaea," or "he sacrificed the Olympia"; it is customary to say also "to sacrifice sacrifices." But it belongs to a worked discourse to set beside it the things from the places — where, and near what, and by whom — as it is in the Anabasis of Cyrus: "And there are also palaces of the Great King at Celaenae, strong, upon the springs of the river Marsyas, beneath the citadel." Then the same resumption, so as to be also another beginning: "and this flows both through the city and falls into the river Maeander." And another distinguished thing again from the place: "Here Apollo is said to have flayed Marsyas, who contended with him about wisdom." That, then, as we said before, one must know about the myths: that it is introduced not as having happened, but as being said to have happened. Then one must know this too, that the ancient manner, whenever it is indeed about very distinguished matters, does not have the same over-elaboration in itself, but it suffices to state the matters and the manner in which they were done, with nothing over-elaborated about them; for to over-elaborate and to linger upon distinguished things draws the discourse away from the ancient mould. "Here it is said" — he did not say, "here is Marsyas a flute-player, a Phrygian by race, to whom it came to think so highly of himself"; for there is lingering and over-elaboration. And see this too: he reversed the order. For the first thing would have been to say that he contended, then that he was defeated, then what he suffered; but in such things, when you reverse the order and set the last first, then so in sequence the things before it, you will make speed and beauty for the discourse; when, after stating what he suffered, the discourse seeks why he suffered: "having contended not about flute-playing or music, but about wisdom." And the skin — another would have said that it hangs, but again that is over-youthful; he says even "to have hung the skin in the cave, whence the springs." Then, as necessary and not over-elaborated, "and on this account the river is called Marsyas." And see in this too the restraint of the ancients; for he did not state the suffering on account of which he added the name of Marsyas to the river, or the misfortune of the flute-player; for Xenophon does none of these things, but it suffices him to say only this much, "and on this account the river is called Marsyas." Then another beginning from a distinguished thing: "Here Xerxes, when, defeated in the battle, he withdrew from Greece." See here too the restraint; for there is no Salamis here, nor fleet and multitude of infantry and triremes, nor how he was defeated, nor how he fled, nor anything else, of all the many things attaching to Xerxes, but bare, "when from Greece." You have learned, then, how the ancients proceed, and how great is the restraint in these things.

Observe this most of all in the thoughts, that one must husband the completing parts and set them last, so that the discourse may share in dignity too. And see this too, that in the simple discourses, even if some of the matters are greater and more esteemed and others lesser, they are always wont to set the lesser first, as here too, though it was a great and distinguished thing that Cyrus gave Clearchus so much money, he did not come at once to this, but first stated the matter of judgement: "he both admired him and gives him ten thousand darics." And the beginning, "Clearchus was a Lacedaemonian exile; Cyrus, having met with him . . ." — the word has a certain marvellous force of character, in not saying, "Cyrus, having made trial of him, or having perceived him to be of great worth and most skilled as a general," but simply, "having met with him." And what follows him, so that the character may most appear, stands thus: "he both admired him and gives him ten thousand darics."

I have often said that comparatives belong to simplicity, for instance, "he loved Cyrus more than the reigning Artaxerxes." As this too: "so as to be friends to him rather than to the King." And to use words less emphatic and to name the smaller in the case of great things belongs to the form of simplicity. In the Anabasis, of Cyrus, "he took care of the barbarians about him" — small namings for a great matter; for "to take care" is proper to none but middling things, and one might say "he takes care of a household," but in the case of an army it is less fitting to use such a word; and in the Agesilaus, "and he himself stayed there again, taking pleasure in the deed." For to use the less emphatic, and not to say "thinking great thoughts" or "lifted up by the victory," but "taking pleasure in the deed," belongs to simplicity.

And the variation of tense belongs to simplicity; for they define the past in the present, for instance, "He summons Cyrus from his command," instead of "he summoned"; for the tense, being changed, made the simplicity. For we must sometimes set down the things that have happened as happening, for instance, "he calls him to the house and converses with him," as though what happened long ago were happening now; and there is novelty in such a thing.

But if you take away from the magnitude by comparatives, it becomes rather elaborateness, as in the Agesilaus, "and the King of the Persians, thinking that Tissaphernes was the cause of all these things, of his affairs going badly, having sent down Tithraustes, cuts off his head"; and this, "cuts off his head," belongs to simplicity, but the "thinking" has a certain disposition of the subject matters; for he did not say, "since the affairs of the barbarians went badly, and so great was the tumult and disorder, and they had been defeated in so many battles, and at last, shut in, were besieged" — nothing of the kind; but he brought out only this, "thinking," and not "both being provoked at what had befallen and considering," but "thinking." And the comparison, "and after this the affairs of the barbarians became more dispirited"; and he did not say, "in dread dispiritedness," but "more dispirited." And to say partitively "the affairs of the barbarians," and not "the barbarians," this too belongs to simplicity, for instance, "who ruled very many cities on the mainland, and ruled islands too."

Further, of the words some are very significative, others less, for instance, the very significative, "he went through," "he drove out"; the less, "he marched," as in the Agesilaus too, "and on the next day, crossing the Achaean mountains of Phthia and all the rest, he marched through a friendly country to the borders of the Boeotians." Novelty too has simplicity; for he transferred the matter of the person onto the place; for instead of saying "through the country of friends" he says "through a friendly country," and instead of "through the country of allies," "through an allied country." The simple writers use also the "here" in varied ways; for it is significative both of place and of time, and the "here" lays hold of the place, while the distension is simple, for it set the thought apart from what preceded. And sometimes he uses a complete demonstrative, "here indeed," sometimes a defective one, "where indeed."

Concerning the trope among the historical writers, one must know only this much: that the tropes must not be taken from great or dignified things, but rather from baser or more ordinary ones, as it is in the Symposium too, "for these men, with their souls purified"; for the word "purified," having a trope from utensils or vessels, transferred from the more ordinary onto the more dignified — onto the men and the soul of the men — has not made the trope clean, but guarded and historical. And such tropes are more habitual to simplicity, for instance, "the land, inhabited and sown, furnishes ever-flowing sustenance." Such a figure belongs very much to the encomiastic kind.

The matters of arrangement must stand so as to seem fitting to each; for in histories the very matters work out also the arrangement of what is said, but in counsels and teachings and memorabilia, as one wishes.

If, then, you have observed these things accurately and trained yourself in them, you will produce, even where there is standing, elaborateness, and from elaborateness standing; and simplicity will be such, in all things possessing the strength of the observations. These things, then, have been sufficiently demonstrated to you concerning what we set before us — all the observations, in each kind of diction, concerning character and the beginnings of discourse and the handling of thoughts and the sweetness of diction, and again the simplicity of diction and narratives and the conduct of myths, and concerning beauty in discourse; and these things have been stated one by one.

As to figure, dignity arises thus: when one uses declarative figures, as in the speech Against Aristogeiton, where Demosthenes says: "The whole life of men, whether they dwell in a small city or a great, is governed by nature and by laws."

As to figure, gravity arises thus, when one uses the figure of thought, for instance: "A fine pair, are they not? — Solon the lawgiver and Timocrates." Or again: "A fine return the multitude of the Oreitae has reaped, in entrusting themselves to Philip's friends and hating Euphraeus! A fine one the people of Eretria, in driving out your envoys and surrendering themselves to Cleitarchus! Indeed, they are slaves now, and are flogged."

As to figure, amplitude arises thus. The hypothetical figure most of all produces amplitude, and so does the use of resultant clauses. What these resultant clauses are in discourse, and how much they can do, you will know from examples, as in the speech Against Conon, right at the beginning: "Having been outraged, gentlemen of the jury, and ill-treated by this man Conon." The simple way would have been to say: "many and dreadful, and indeed various, things, than which none has been more dreadful." But by means of the resultant clause he produced amplitude: "such that for a very long time neither my relatives nor any of the physicians expected me to survive." There is a difference also in the special quality of the resultant clause; for to this attend closely: if he had said simply, "Having been outraged, gentlemen of the jury, and ill-treated by Conon many and dreadful things," the thought would have been complete and would have needed nothing, and one would have had to pass on; but to suspend it upon the resultant clause, in saying "and having suffered such things," had as its consequence the addition: "of what sort? — such that for a very long time neither my relatives nor any of the physicians expected me to survive." The resultant clause, then, has this power: to make many things out of a single word, and to produce amplitude. And again in the speech Against Conon, going on, he says: "And at first they reviled me, but at last they laid blows upon me as well." The simple way would have been to say, "and they made a great outcry and uproar about the tent"; but the thought would have been complete and like something flung down. As it is, the resultant clause produced the amplitude: "and they made so great an outcry and uproar about the tent" — for upon the suspension by the resultant clause there necessarily follows the addition of another thought — "such that the general too and the taxiarchs came." And there is another resultant clause in the speech: the simple way would have been to say, "they put me in a sorry state, leaping upon me and striking me"; but the amplitude from the resultant clause is: "they put me in such a state, leaping upon me and striking me, that they split my lip."

As to figure, credibility arises thus: when one uses figures proper to admitted things instead of disputed ones, as there: "Do you see and reckon up the coming season of the year, into which certain men think you must leave the Hellespont desolate?" And again, for the sake of credibility, he introduces by means of the figure something as admitted: "For you surely know this, that of those who wrong you a single assessment is fixed for each." And again: "You know perhaps, even without a word from me, that Chabrias was a worthy man."

As to figure, vehemence arises thus, when one uses aggressive figures, for instance: "A shameful law, men of Athens, and a bad one, and like something born of envy and contentiousness." And again: "Bar him, then, bar him from speaking on behalf of the peace." And in the speech Against Meidias: "And though I suffer these things, and am being driven, in the manner I am now describing to you." And in the speech On the False Embassy: "Than these things, men of Athens, nothing more dreadful has happened."

As to figure, emphasis arises when one uses demonstratives, for instance: "This law, men of Athens, is both ancient and good." And again, in deliberative speeches: "Look at this city, great in size as it is." "Do you see Aristolochus the son of Charidemus? Once he had an estate; then now there are many to whom he was in debt; it was while he owed them that he acquired it."

There are also other figures concerning discourse, and likewise concerning poetry, both far from and near to one another, which it is not easy to grasp all at once; but each man, taking off a portion, has won repute in respect of that — though I except Homer the poet from the discussion. When, then, one makes it a feat to go through all these fine things and to mingle all the minglings in discourse, one must first render the characters suited to the occasions; then the conjunctions — where there is precision, there adding charm; where brevity, there speed; to the abundant, clarity; grace where dignity is; where there is invention, there management; where there are bold strokes, there safety. And here every hearer is dizzied and does not know what is to become of him; but, as in a battle-line men surrounded are thrown into confusion, so each, according to the nature he has, praises one thing or another: the one the precision of the diction, another the subtlety of the sense, another that it is graceful, another something else.

Not one thing alone hinders us from recalling the expedition from Sicily, but first, that one must not change and alter one's resolves easily — for that is a dreadful thing. And you will amplify this in the quality of the person addressed: "But for you it is not even, on equal terms, as shameful as for all the others. Why? Because you are trusted to have more wisdom than the rest." And again another amplification from the matter, that you did not deliberate about these affairs simply, nor for a short time; and here you will set beside it the things drawn from history. Against these, the first antithesis: "But Sicily is hard to take." This too we knew was said before — both how great its size is and how great the voyage round it — and yet we sent the expedition. But indeed it is not even hard to take; for its inhabitants are at faction and at war with one another. What, then, is hard in taking an island divided both in its preparations and in its counsels? But we have stumbled. Yet one must not so easily give way in spirit; and this you will establish from a like case that occurred among the Syracusans themselves, that they too, having stumbled not once but many times, recovered themselves; and if they did, so will you. What absurdity, then, comes of their changing course? First, shame — not only at having deliberated badly, but at seeming less manly than the Syracusans; then you will make the Syracusans despise you. "But the Lacedaemonians have broken the truce." Yet not even then did we appear to take courage from these truces. "But the fort they have raised against us is something new." What then? Do you think that, going there, they will overpower the Lacedaemonians? And indeed, if they stay within, it may perhaps be even to our advantage as well; for it is no benefit to the besieged to bring in a great crowd of men. What goods will come to them from taking Sicily? "But Gylippus is gathering an army and mustering Sicily." Then what befitted you was not to flee in fear, but rather to send out another fleet, which will furnish our citizens with a desire no less than Gylippus furnishes the Syracusans; for our men will have not only the strength, but the consciousness of having often prevailed, while those who think to set right the former state by their numbers, then appear weaker in their preparations, will, I think, with good reason become inferior in spirit as well. The remaining inquiry is from the outcomes. "What more will there be, even if we prevail? For we shall not be able to hold it, being far off." But I could wish that your affairs stood thus, since to hold it and to guard it is secure. And you might say, violently and in the manner of Demosthenes, that it is not even possible to do anything else; for we shall seem not to be withdrawing but to be fleeing, and not as men unable to take it, but as men afraid to suffer; then the Syracusans will not refrain from pursuing us; and if this comes about, I fear the danger may be over the Piraeus itself, and we may admit enemy ships into our own harbours, when we ought to be blockading others. Such, then, are the things, and in such terms.

There were lambs, well-nourished and thick with fleece, marvellous in beauty and in size. These I took and bound quietly together, three by three; for there were those on which the Cyclops slept, and the middle one was to carry one of my comrades, while one on either side ran beside it as a trace-horse, for safety's sake. For the others, then, these served me; but I myself set about it in the following way. There was a ram, beyond all others huge and exceedingly shaggy; about him I threw both my hands along his back and lay hidden under his belly, until I too came to be there; then, turning round, I clung fast. So through that night, faring thus hard, we held out.

Or when one uses the figure of detachment. The nature of this figure of detachment is of the following kind: when, departing from the practice of linking things in sequence and binding them to one another, we bring them back to a fresh beginning of their own, so that what was joined among the conceptions is severed and stands apart — as in the Philippics, in the speech Against Philip, where the point to be established is: "Philip is acting outrageously; for he does this and that," for instance, "He has enslaved Thessaly; the cities in Euboea are already under tyrants; he has gone off against the Hellespont; before that he came against Ambracia; he holds Elis, so great a city in the Peloponnese." Then comes the heightening: "And while he does such things, none of the Greeks hinders him," among which he says also this: "And the Greeks, knowing these things, send no embassies about them, and feel no indignation." And at the end: "So that, while he is doing such things, what are we ourselves doing?" Then there is the heightening drawn from contrast: "And this, when our ancestors would yield none of these things even to the barbarians, nor indeed to the most distinguished of the Greeks — not to the Lacedaemonians, not to the Athenians, not, in the end, to the Thebans." Then, upon all this, comes the giving of the cause: "What, then, is the cause of these things?" Here now attend to the figure of detachment; for I have gone through all this first for the sake of clarity. If he had wished to bring out the established thought in linked form, he would have done it thus: "Whereas they all hated those who took money from men wishing to rule or to corrupt Greece, this man does not do so." But, breaking the linkage of the thoughts and detaching it from being joined to itself, he brings it back to a beginning and says: "There was something then — there was, men of Athens — in the minds of the many." What was this? "All hated those who took money from men wishing to rule or to corrupt Greece." Then something else came about by the figure, though it is one and the same conception, whether I state it in linked form — "What, then, is the cause of these things? That those men were not of this mind" — or whether, using detachment, I bring it back: "There was something then — there was — in the minds of the many." And elsewhere, using a forewarning, I shall say: "But I will speak with frankness; for indeed I could not do otherwise." Then, detaching, he adds: "All who have ever sailed forth from you as generals." And these too are figures of detachment: "It is a fine thing, men of Athens, a fine thing, the guarding of public affairs"; and that, set against it: "A foul thing, men of Athens, a foul thing is this beast, and unsociable." It is not because countless other observations are not present in each of these observations that I have not mentioned them by kind; for in some of them there has also been a doubling, and in general the matter has been brought out as a whole and not in part. But our purpose is to demonstrate one by one each of the generic figures, and so you yourself requested. And in general, upon a single conception many observations often coincide — especially such of them as are of the same kindred — and from these the discourse, when it is perfectly furnished in all its parts, draws something further: in thought, in figure, in rhythm, in diction. But our concern now is only with figure itself, and at that only with the figure of thought. There are also other forms of detachment, for instance: "Meidias will suffer nothing terrible or pitiable if he comes to have what most of you have"; and again: "Many rich men banded together, having gained, through their wealth, the appearance of being persons of some importance"; and again: "Meidias perhaps hates me."

To gravity belongs also the use of plaintive figures, for instance: "Charidemus — alas!" And that saying of Aeschines: "You endured it utterly, like men of iron." And reticences will avail you to the same end, for instance: "What could one rightly call you, that would name you aright?"

A figure of amplitude is also that of enumeration. An example of this is in the speech On the False Embassy, where he says: "Of what, then, must one demand an account from an envoy?" The simple way would have been to say, "of what he reported, of what he persuaded"; but the amplitude lies in the enumeration: "first, then, of what he reported; second, of what he persuaded; third, of what you commissioned him to do." And again elsewhere: "For what purpose, then, did I go through these things? First, that you might know and learn; second, for a purpose no less important than this."

Credible as to figure is also when one uses an undertaking in the discourse; for it is very credible to give a pledge concerning the matters in dispute, as in the speech Against Leptines: the point at issue is whether they will enact the proposed law; and he gives a pledge, saying: "We undertake — I, Phormio, and any other he wishes — to propose the law." And again: "We undertake, we promise; let the lawgivers draw these things up; on these terms let the matter proceed."

Vehemence is found also in the figure of apostrophe: "You, foulest of all men, when your freedom of speech is barred — not by railings or doors, which someone might open a little, but by such great and so many debts, and these lodged in the keeping of the goddess — you force your way within these and approach those things from which the laws drive you off, fenced out from all the rights in the city." And again in the speech Against Meidias: "What do you say, you foul fellow? — will you think fit to ask pity for your own children, or that these men pity you, the men whom you have publicly dragged through the mud?"

Questions, too, will produce emphasis for you, as in the speech Against Boeotus, On the Name: "But if someone should ask you, 'Boeotus, how is it that you now belong to the tribe Acamantis, and the deme Thoricus, and are the son of Mantitheus?' — you could say nothing else but that 'Mantitheus while still living adopted me too.'" And in the speech On the Crown: "But if you disbelieve, ask them — or rather I shall do this for you" — then the question: "Does Aeschines seem to you, men of Athens, to be a hireling of Alexander, or his guest-friend?"

And since the parts of virtue too are found in the form of rhetoric, the orator would also be such a man. For it belongs, I think, to the prudent and temperate man to know the worth of each of the matters; to the just man, to render what is fitting both to himself and to others; to the brave man, not to be afraid to speak the truth; and the same man feels indignation at all that is opposite to these. With reason some are held to this, lest it should seem that the words are alien to the speaker, drawing after them a reputation greater than the truth. It belongs, then, to the orator to do these things too: to discern what is best, and to express it, and to manage each thing; to keep the harmonies and the order and the choice always fitting to the occasion; to chasten, to exhort, to restrain, to bring in whatever is needful; and altogether to render his discourses partakers of beauty and of sense and of strength and of temperance, by the density of the enthymemes, the symmetry of the words, the harmonies, the depth of thought, the figures, and the graces of the headings, of the intention, and of the themes.

Distensions, too, have dignity, as when he says: "What, then, does he attempt? To make war upon the Amphictyons, and to stir up confusion about the Pylaea." For without the distension it would run thus: "For Philip reasoned that, if he should persuade either the Thessalians or the Thebans to march against you for the sake of his own private enmity, no one would heed him; but that, if he took up their common grievances and were chosen leader, he would more easily hope to deceive in some things, and in others to win over whomever he might. What, then? He makes war upon the Amphictyons, and stirs up confusion about the Pylaea." That would be the form without the distension — confused and lowly; but to raise it to dignity is the work of the distension set in the middle: "What, then, does he attempt?" and then the matter coming after the distension: "to make war upon the Amphictyons." And elsewhere: "The worst feature in what is past is, in regard to the future, the best." Here, too, without the distension, the immediate sequel would be: "For though we do none of the things we ought." Where, then, is the distension? In the clause set between, in which, distending, he says: "What, then, is this? — that we do none of the things we ought." But these are divisions according to the matter — "What, then, does he attempt?" or again, "What, then, is this?" — while those others arise from a kind of self-judgement, as when he says: "For indeed it is so: I have been outraged, and my body was then defiled." And there always attends upon the distension this too, that it makes the discourse well-articulated, and in some places clear as well. One must know that the observations of discourse bring with them great beauty; but for now we are dealing with one, the most generic.

Gravity arises also when you are led to say something painful against the hearers, which one would suppose they would bear ill, and then you set it right, as though having nothing more moderate to say of it — as in the letters: "But if you look to the conspicuous dignity of the Council or of the Areopagus, then, remembering the trial of Aristogeiton, hide your faces; for I have no gentler form of address for those who have sinned against me."

Praeteritions, too, produce amplitude, as in the speech Against Meidias: "All the trouble, then, that he gave, opposing our being released from the campaign on behalf of the chorus-members, or putting himself forward to be elected overseer for the Dionysia, and all the other such things — I shall pass over." And again: "That he framed an indictment of desertion against me, and hired the man who did it — that foul and utterly shameless fellow, that dust-cloud, Euctemon — I shall pass over." One must know that some praeteritions are indefinite, others by species. Indefinite are such as these: "Everything I could not state to you, nor would you wish to hear, all that he received as gifts from both sides" — and the generic form especially produces this effect. Such praeteritions, then, in their indefiniteness produce amplitude; but the praeteritions by species are like this: "Olynthus, indeed, and Apollonia and thirty-two cities in Thrace I pass over." And some praeteritions occur at the beginning, like this one, "Olynthus, indeed, and Apollonia," while others at the end, as where he says: "and his campaigns against the Illyrians and Paeonians and wherever one might mention, I pass over." Of those at the end there is also this praeterition, which possesses amplitude: "Though I have many other things as well to set forth that have been done by these men, and they have been proved liars, I would gladly tell you; but since you suppose it to be beside the point, I shall pass it over." And you will increase amplitude if you do not state the praeteritions bare, but add their justifications as well, as in the speech Against Leptines: "In what way, then, with you well-disposed toward all the Peloponnesians, he drew them up in array at Thebes, and how he slew Gorgopas in Aegina, and all that he did in Cyprus, and after that in Egypt, and that, having traversed almost the whole country, nowhere did he disgrace the name of the city or himself" — and the justification for which he passes over it: "because it is impossible to speak in accordance with his deserts, and there is much shame, when I speak of these things, that they should appear less than the opinion of him existing in each man's mind."

To credibility belongs also when one uses concurrences, as in the Philippics, for instance: "But if it seems to anyone that these things involve much expense and trouble" — now the concurrence, and very rightly so. For he first concedes what seems to be against himself, in order to introduce what is in his favour.
And when one uses continuous denials, emphasis arises in the discourse.

For some discourses are panegyric, some deliberative, some forensic. Of the forensic, some turn on essence, some on particular character, some on quality; and again, of the forensic discourses some, I think, are very short, some very long, some between these. The deliberative are by nature shorter than the forensic — although there are deliberative discourses, as it were, longer than the forensic, and forensic discourses than those of the same kind, and others near them in extent; but neither are these set down apart from those, nor do those differ at all from these. For by the chance of the circumstances they advance both to a lesser and to a greater length, each beyond itself and beyond the other, while by their whole nature the one is somewhat more than the other. And this is a sign that the deliberative is not much shorter than the longest contentious speech, so that the contests aim to be distinguished from one another not only in their figures but also in their proportion, broadly speaking; the man deliberating, then, will say all that is needful, but will say it in fewer words than the one contending a suit; while the one contending will say everything, just as the one deliberating.

A figure of dignity arises also when one uses obliqueness. For where the thoughts are set upright, the discourse is chopped up one by one, and the figure belongs rather to the purer manner than to the more dignified; on this account, in the speech Against Leptines, so long as Demosthenes keeps the thoughts upright, the discourse seems pure, as: "The Thirty are said to have borrowed money from the Lacedaemonians against those in the Piraeus." Another thought of the same manner: "And when those affairs were settled, the Lacedaemonians sent envoys and demanded the money back." And what follows, had he carried it forward in the same manner, he would have said thus: "Discussions then arose, and some thought those from the city should repay the money, others those from the Piraeus." But the tone of the figure, and the dignity, would have been destroyed; and so, using obliqueness, he says: "And when discussions arose, some bidding those from the city to repay, others those in the Piraeus, this proved the first sign of concord." And at the opening of the speech Against Philip: "Though many discussions arise, men of Athens, about the wrongs Philip is committing." And another thing rendered oblique upon this: "And which all, I well know, would have said." And again: "And though our present circumstances, men of Athens, are, as I judge, fearful to all, none are in greater danger than you."

Gravity has also this quality: when, having granted something as belonging to you, you then take it away and cast doubt upon it — as in the Philippics: "But he, while you remained at home, idle, in good health" — having granted this as belonging to them, he at once took it away with a qualification: "if indeed we are to call those who do such things 'in good health.'"

Most of all do partitions produce amplitude, when you do not bring in the thoughts singly, but, dividing them, set them in opposition, as in the Philippics: "But if the one shall have resolved that he must always be doing something greater than what he has, while you shall have resolved that you must take hold of nothing." This thought, then, may be divided into persons; but another may be divided into person and place: "When, then, you cannot sail up from here, and there is no help ready there." Isocrates very much delights in producing amplitude by this kind of partition; and, for the sake of an example, here are one or two from the On the Peace of Isocrates: "For we have come to this point" — and the partition — "of negligence toward our own affairs and of desire for what belongs to others"; then, stating the absurd results that befell them from these, he partitions: "They filled the public tombs with citizens, and the phratries and the registers with foreigners." Then again, recounting what befell the Lacedaemonians as a result of their empire by sea, he says: "The sea filled them" — the private men with "injustice, lawlessness, indolence, love of money" — and the common body of the city he did not simply set against "this and that," but again subdivided: "and the common body of the city with arrogance toward some, and desire for what belonged to others." But subdivisions too can produce amplitude, for instance: "You have not only done this, but that also" — "not only of cities and lands, of which we were once masters, do you appear to be letting go, but also of the allies and opportunities furnished by fortune." And in the speech Against Leptines: "It is not, then, only that Leucon should not be wronged that we must consider, but anyone else as well" — this being the case introduced concerning Epicerdes. And again: "It is not, then, only those who privately resolved to do you good, men of Athens, and showed themselves useful, that it is right to take care not to wrong, but many also who furnished whole cities, their own fatherlands, as allies to us in the war against the Lacedaemonians." And again: "It is not, then, only Conon who was honoured by us at that time for doing what I have recounted, but by many others as well."

Very credible too is this, when one uses praeteritions. The figure is, indeed, also one of amplitude; nevertheless, fitting many uses to different needs, it often has a certain special force in credibility. For when, seeming to pass something over, you do not pass it over, there is credibility, as in the speech Against Leptines: "As for the other things, all the ways in which this man showed himself useful, both he and his ancestors" — then he used praeterition — "I shall pass over." And again: "A shameful law, men of Athens, and a bad one, like something born of envy and contentiousness" — then, having nothing more to say, credibly he used praeterition: "and the rest I let go."

There being, then, three kinds of discourse, and the chance of the circumstances concerning them being what it is, I say that other kinds fall into the same discourse, which one must take up and blend — as the speech of Demosthenes, the one that gives the guard to Charidemus, partakes somewhere of the three kinds. For the part about the illegality is, of itself, outright forensic, refuting Aristocrates because he has moved something contrary to the laws; the part again about the expedient has a certain deliberative cast, that one must not allow Cersobleptes to grow greater; and a third upon these belongs to the panegyric manner — the censure of Charidemus. All these come round into the one, the forensic, and there has been a certain blending and mingling of them of this kind; and neither is the one such as the other, but each differs only so far as the matter wills, and the kinds are not at all torn apart from one another, so that the whole discourse is not at variance with itself.

This must be known first concerning the figures: that there is a certain partnership in discourse between elevation and dignity. For where the discourse takes on elevation, there it takes on dignity as well. Let the discourse be directed to matters of thought; the use of similes, further, makes the discourse possess dignity and elevation, as: "Like a fitful wind upon the sea, moving as chance directs"; and again: "Like a thunderbolt or a torrent, this whole affair fell upon the city"; and elsewhere again: "Since, that, like the period or onset of a fever or some other illness, it comes even upon him who now thinks himself very far removed — of this no one is ignorant."
And perplexities within lamentations have gravity, as in the letters: "Ah, what could I say that would seem neither to err nor to lie? — Far too negligent!"

Amplitude belongs also to introducing the thoughts by way of juxtaposition, when one does not simply say "this happened and that," but, instead of "this happening," "this happened," and instead of "that," "that" — as Demosthenes in the speech On the False Embassy: "For instead of seeing Thespiae and Plataea resettled, you heard of Orchomenus and Coronea being enslaved." And Isocrates too delights in producing amplitude by the figure of juxtaposition: "For instead of garrisoning the citadels of others, they saw the enemy masters of their own; instead of taking the children of others as hostages, they say they saw their own being reared in unworthy fashion; instead of tilling the lands of others, for many years they could not even see their own."
And to speak against oneself in the same way one speaks against the adversaries instils credibility into the discourse.

One must know that the themes of deliberative questions are these: the just, the expedient, the possible, the easy, the necessary, the safe, the honourable, the pious, the holy, the pleasant, and their opposites. The just is constituted by law, by nature, by custom; and the just by law is considered in command and in prohibition. The expedient is constituted from four sources, which are these: the keeping of the goods we have, the gaining of goods we do not have, the escape from present evils, the prevention of impending evils. The possible is constituted from persons and from what is applied to them. The easy is constituted from these: that it requires fewer toils or less expense or fewer dangers or something of the sort, as against the contrary. The necessary is constituted from a man's not being able, evidently, to do what he wishes otherwise than as necessity compels; from escaping fears and disturbances and griefs and the violence in necessities otherwise than in this way, or as necessity compels; from the thing being defined as wholly necessary, such as dying. The safe is constituted from these: that there is no fear of suffering anything, neither from gods nor from enemies nor from any stronger persons nor from the law. The honourable is constituted, to embrace it in a definition, from the praises of good things. These are: the pious, honours, praises, memorials, friendships, trusts, the reputations of ancestors, and what attaches to deeds, which one must not disgrace, and the keeping of what is fitting in life — such as good order, simplicity, truth, friendship; and it would belong here too if, besides these, the honourable is also constituted from praising and comparing the deeds of others. And in general, all that is according to virtue and the works of virtue: for all these belong to the honourable. And the opposites are set against these. The pious is constituted from the natural observance of the rights and customs toward the gods. The holy is constituted from the keeping of the rights toward the fatherland and its forethought, and toward parents and benefactors and teachers and those beneath the earth. The pleasant is constituted from the enjoyment of pleasures; and of pleasures some arise from taste, some from sight, some from hearing, some according to the understanding, which last happen to be the greater and the purer.
The uttering of maxims, too, belongs to dignity, as: "For prosperity beyond one's deserts becomes, for the foolish, a starting-point for thinking ill."

Amplitude is produced also by completions, as in the speech Against Conon: "That, then, it was no moderate or trifling blows I received" — and the opposite of "no trifling blows I received" — "but, by coming back because of these men's outrage and wantonness" — he goes on, "having suffered what, I have done what?" — "I have brought a far lighter suit than was fitting"; now the gathering clause, to a heightening, admitted: "from many sources I think it has become plain to you." But since I have already, for you who are following along, demonstrated the several observations of amplitude in the cases where the completion occurred — for to set down the completion itself would be of this kind: "That, then, it was no moderate or trifling blows I received, but, coming back because of these men's outrage and wantonness, I have brought a far lighter suit than was fitting, I think has become plain to you." There are also other completions that produce a marvellous amplitude, at once completing and rounding off what has been said before and providing a transition to what is introduced next, as in the speech On the Crown: "The things, then, that I furnished toward the justice of writing such things about me — besides many others, these and the like are they"; thus far the completion; then the announcement of what follows: "but the things that you all know, these I shall now state."

As for the panegyric kind, since it lies outside of questions at issue, its themes are either from persons or from matters, from which come both praises and encomia and hymns, and their opposites, censures. Of the laudatory kinds, then, one is called praise, one a hymn, one an encomium: a hymn is to the gods, having nothing of the opposite in it; praise is what is bestowed upon small things, such as "well" and "fairly" — for these too are laudatory — and again, "the good man," "the brave," "the just"; the encomium raises to something greater, and on this account they proceed by a full treatment. Praises are taken according to four modes: by amplification, by omission, by comparison, by fair speaking. By amplification, for instance, if one should wish, in praising the works of the ant, to say that it is most thrifty in the gathering of the harvest and in the storing of it, and moreover good at foreseeing the seasons sent by the gods and most prudent in preparing against the right times — and all that one might find in magnifying the ant. By omission, when, omitting the disagreeable things that attach to those being praised and that one might mention in censure, we report only the things worthy of praise — for instance, if, in praising Alexander, we should recount his other deeds: how he crossed the Granicus, how he advanced as far as Cilicia, how he subdued all the nations as far as the Ocean, but should omit the slaying of Cleitus and his addiction to drinking-bouts, and that he changed into Median dress and thought fit to be worshipped like the King of the Persians, and all such things as he had. By comparison, when, wishing to make the things of the one praised appear greater, we demonstrate it from comparison with other things, as Demosthenes, wishing to show that the works of Conon concerning the building of the walls were great, says they were better than those of Themistocles. By fair speaking, when, without omitting the disagreeable things, we report them in a fairer light, for instance, if, praising Alexander, we should say of the seizure of Helen, not that it was a wrong or an adultery or any sin against Menelaus the host, but that he desired to become a kinsman of Zeus; and again, of Helen, that she did not err in leaving her husband and her daughter and her home, but that she was eager to become renowned.

To cast out and do away with the less esteemed things and bring in instead the more esteemed belongs to dignity: "I walled the city neither with stones nor with bricks; but if you wish to learn my fortification, you will find it to be the things more highly esteemed — arms, and cities, and lands, and harbours."

And to render the thoughts oblique belongs most of all to amplitude; so that even in narratives, if the thoughts be made oblique, it produces marvellous amplitude, as Demosthenes in the speech Against Aeschines: and having Ischander, the second actor of Neoptolemus, he did not set it upright by saying "he approached the Council," but again made it oblique: "and approaching the Council, and approaching the people about these matters." And another rendered oblique: "and having persuaded you to send envoys everywhere about these matters." And another of the same manner: "and reporting." And another upon these: "and going through how grievously they wrong all Greece, not only their own fatherlands, those who take bribes and money from Philip." But how did Aeschines do it?
