"For when Amyntas had lately died" — and another obliqueness — "and Alexander, the elder of the brothers, while Perdiccas and Philip were still children" — and another obliqueness: "and Pausanias was coming down to claim their throne, being an exile, but strong through the occasion" — and again another obliqueness upon another: "and many were cooperating with him, and he had a Greek force, and had taken Anthemus and Therma, while the Macedonians were not of one mind, but most of them inclined to the cause of Pausanias — at this juncture" — "he set us upright and gave us rest, the Athenians chose Iphicrates as general."

Of praising not coarsely, but being able to do it in as many ways as need arises in political questions, the modes are these. First, when one seems to have been brought to it not as one who plotted and prepared it himself, but as one compelled. Second, when one rejects some things and goes through others. A third mode, when, before saying anything, one asks pardon of the judges for what one is about to say. Fourth, when one keeps the praise within common matters. Fifth, when one declares that it befits the hearers themselves to accept it. Sixth, when one is able to show the adversaries doing the same thing, and declares it a dreadful thing that they should do it for their own advantage, but oneself not.

The discourse has dignity also when you do not at once run upon what is being introduced, but take up beforehand the forces of the matters and suspend the discourse upon them: "One safeguard the nature of sensible men possesses in itself, common to all." And he did not at once go on and say "distrust," but having first taken up the forces of this thing and suspended his sentence upon them: "which is for all a good and a means of safety, but most of all for the multitude against tyrants." And another resumption: "What, then, is this?" — and then the thing introduced: "distrust." Like to this is the following also: "the very thing that both prevailed over the wealth of the Persians and kept Greece free, and was beaten neither in battle by sea nor by land — but now, being lost, it has ruined everything and turned all affairs upside down." And though so much is set forth beforehand, the "what" has not yet been stated; but using resumption, he will now bring it in: "What, then, was this?" — and then the thing introduced by itself, as there "distrust," so here: "All hated those who took money from men wishing to rule or to corrupt Greece."

Concerning censure. Censure is taken in three modes; for one may censure by amplification, by omission, and by comparison — but not by fair speaking; rather, by the opposite of fair speaking, foul speaking. Censure arises by foul speaking when things well done are reported in a fouler light, for instance, if one should say that Menelaus marched against Troy not over great matters, not indignant over the things in which the barbarian outraged Greece, but for the sake of a single woman, and that not a good one, as the tragic poet too says: "O man who would lead an army for a woman's sake, and for nothing else."
Definitions, too, that are set in the universal have dignity, as: "For my part, I count as a city's wealth its allies, its trust, its goodwill."

And always to keep stepping back, leading what is distinguished — whether persons or matters — away from oneself, is very dignified, as: "And of these things none is new, nor any discovery of mine; but an ancient law, which this man has transgressed, prescribes lawmaking thus"; and again: "I am not speaking words of my own, but the records of your ancestors."

This too is a figure of dignity: to set the thoughts side by side without connectives, placing them one after another, as: "Meidias of Anagyrus has put himself forward; he knows the secrets; the city cannot contain him." And again: "He has gone off against the Hellespont; before that he came against Ambracia; he holds Elis, so great a city in the Peloponnese; lately he plotted against Megara; neither Greece nor the barbarian world can contain the man's grasping."

As to diction, dignity arises thus: when one uses substantive expressions instead of verbal ones, as: "A great advantage, men of Athens, accrued to Philip." And: "For reckless daring was accounted bravery, a friend's part."

As to diction, amplitude arises thus: when one uses equivalent expressions. One must know that of equivalents some are set side by side as consequents, others as opposites of the consequent. As consequents, where he says: "You are vigorous and trust yourself"; and again, "his wantonness and his outrage"; and again, "his wealth and his abundance," or "his comrades and friends." As opposites of the consequent, equivalents again are these: "seeing these things neglected and meeting with no help." An equivalent too is that: "all of you and the whole people."

As to delivery — that is, as to diction — vehemence arises when you employ hyperboles in the discourse, for instance: "rich, bold, high-minded, loud-voiced, violent, shameless." And it has hyperbole also when you say: "The city cannot contain him." "Neither Greece nor the barbarian world can contain the man's grasping." And where he says: "To do obeisance to those who commit outrage, as among the barbarians, and not to defend ourselves, will be best."
As to delivery, emphasis arises in the same manner as harshness and vehemence do.

And when you use figurative expressions instead of proper ones, as to call bribery a disease: "A disease, men of Athens, dread, has fallen upon Greece." And elsewhere again: "Then the man who sets up this engine against the city." And in the speech Against Meidias: "But you, having become the contributor to such a fund, justly deserve to collect this from yourself."

And one must know that this observation, too, is second to none: that dignity and amplitude have everything in common; for in all the ways in which they are constituted, they share with one another, and one must think of them in this way.

All these things produce vehemence in the discourse by heightening it, as in the speech Against Conon: "I was dragged and stripped, and, coming out unsound, I was carried home on a litter"; and where he speaks about his mother — for he did not say "she had come out," but, more emphatically by the word, "his mother had leaped forth"; for in the word lies the emphasis.
To speak in the plural, and to set the names one after another, belongs to dignity, as: "Prosperous and great and terrible to all, Greeks and barbarians."

And as we have often said that tropes in many places have great power, this holds in vehemence too, when, for the sake of vehemence, he says against the baseness of Aristogeiton: "a huckster and trafficker, who all but kept his scales and weights and sold everything."

To remove the persons and carry the discourse forward upon the very matters is exceedingly dignified: "If Thespiae and Plataea and the prospect that the Thebans should presently pay the penalty had not taken away the truth" — but it was those who spoke of the affairs of the Thespians and Plataeans; he, however, removing the persons of those who said these things, speaks of them in the abstract: "If Thespiae and Plataea . . ." And elsewhere again: "But I think you should not have to persuade yourselves to keep the peace" — and he stated the opposite: "but Philip" — yet, removing the person, he spoke of the matter indefinitely: "but the one who is carrying on the business of war." And again elsewhere, wishing to show that it is Philip who is making the war, instead of saying so outright: "But if Philip, holding arms in his hands and having much force about him" — whereas the other man said it directly.

To dignity belongs also the use of more generic names. By "generic" I mean "gold," "silver"; for from these is derived what is said of species and part — "money," "wealth," "revenue." Thucydides, raising these to the generic, produced dignity; Hermocrates says of the Carthaginians: "For they have gold and silver in greatest quantity," instead of "for they are very rich," or, transposed otherwise, "for they are rich." And Demosthenes, instead of saying, "Arthmius was punished because he corrupted certain men with money in the Peloponnese," by speaking generically — "because he brought gold from the King" — produced dignity.

One must know that dignity arises even from a single word, as in the speech Against Leptines, where he says that one must keep the inscribed pillars in force. How did he raise it to dignity? In the last word: "that those pillars may be a memorial of the character of the city."
